paras.en: Because individual states have the power to prosecute crimes and order executions, much of the power lies with state governor.
paras.zh: 由于各州有权起诉犯罪并下令处决，因此大部分权力属于州长。

paras.en: The decision comes after the high-profile botched execution of a woman in Tennessee last month and while executions have been on the rise in the US.
paras.zh: 这一决定是在上个月田纳西州一名妇女被高调拙劣处决之后做出的，而美国的处决数量一直在增加。

paras.en: On the federal level, President Donald Trump, a long-time supporter of the death penalty, has described capital punishment as "an essential tool for deterring and punishing those who would commit the most heinous crimes and acts of lethal violence against American citizens".
paras.zh: 在联邦层面，长期支持死刑的唐纳德·特朗普总统将死刑描述为“威慑和惩罚那些对美国公民犯下最令人发指的罪行和致命暴力行为的重要工具”。

paras.en: In 2020, during his first term, he ended a nearly two-decade moratorium on the federal death penalty, by ordering 13 executions over a six month period.
paras.zh: 2020 年，在他的第一个任期内，他下令在六个月内处决 13 人，结束了联邦近两年暂停执行死刑的状态。

paras.en: While the moratorium returned under President Biden, on the first day of Trump's second term in 2025, he signed an executive order that re-instated the death penalty.
paras.zh: 虽然拜登总统重新暂停执行死刑，但在特朗普 2025 年第二任期的第一天，他签署了一项恢复死刑的行政命令。

paras.en: No federal executions have been carried out since he signed it, however. In the US, both the federal government and local states authorities can order executions.
paras.zh: 然而，自他签署该协议以来，联邦尚未执行任何处决。在美国，联邦政府和地方政府都可以下令执行死刑。

articles.title: Off-Highway Brake & Friction Excellence is All-Italian

paras.en: Off-Highway Brake & Friction Excellence is All-Italian

SK Wellman, a company specializing in the production of brake and frictions components for off-highway, has a lively DNA. A historical reality in Orzinuovi (Bs), where the plant is still located, over the years it has undergone transformations and changes that have contributed to making it what it is today: an evolved company, able to grow in loyalty to the local Italian territory and to innovate its sector with creativity and flexibility worldwide. Today, as part of the CentroMotion Group and its Carlisle Brake & Friction division, SK Wellman is a leader in its segment, recognized and chosen by major brands in earthmoving, agricultural and construction machinery. Engineer Alessandro Gamba, Global Director of Friction Engineering, tells us about the ongoing growth.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: "S.K. Wellman S.R.L. has 340 employees and a turnover of 127 million by 2023," Gamba begins. In the last five years, a strong push has come from the market but above all from the characteristics of SK, such as creativity, innovation, flexibility, which, in the final analysis, are the result of the greatest wealth of this company: people". They are the ones who make the Brescia-based company an authentic and tenacious company, to the point of being able to export not only their products successfully, but also their skills and design skills to the other plants of the Carlisle Brake & Friction division. The year 2023, which has just ended, confirms a positive performance in turnover for sales revenues alone, recording a slight decrease of -5% compared to the previous exceptional 2022 financial year; A year, the latter, probably unrepeatable for many realities of the Brescia and non-Brescia economy. In fact, 2023 was undoubtedly the year of change that helped people develop a greater ability to manage uncertainty, accepting and dealing with unexpected situations with more resilience.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: "At the base of success there is a matrix organization developed thanks to group governance - explains the engineer -: a verticality driven on all functions and skills, able to define and guide processes on a global scale and generate best practices. And that's not all," adds Gamba, "we are one of the companies with the lowest level of turnover, and this allows us to transfer the experience of those who have been with us for a long time to young people, on whom we particularly focus. Added to this is a company population of 15 different nationalities, whose strong collaboration creates a truly serene working climate," says the HR Manager. It is no coincidence that the direction of growth is particularly social responsibility.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: "Among the main projects of SK Wellman and Carlisle - he observes - stands out Enactus, an international non-profit organization that, thanks to its activity, involves university students in the creation of sustainable entrepreneurial projects, helping to bridge the gap between university and business; and then Treedom, which involves the company's commitment to planting 1,600 trees in three years, involving its stakeholders in the project". Two more rare gems for the metalworking industry? A level of accidents at work that borders on zero, and the centrality of talent development. Towards excellence and beyond.

articles.title: A Holiday Season of Giving

paras.en: This holiday season, Carlisle Brake & Friction’s Medina location is proud to support 15 children of our colleagues who could use a little extra cheer. Our employees have generously donated toys, clothing, and other essential items to bring joy to these young lives.

By coming together as a team, we’re demonstrating our commitment to making a positive impact on our community. We’re grateful for the kindness and generosity of our employees, and we hope this initiative will bring warmth and happiness to the children who receive these gifts.

Want to join us in spreading holiday cheer? Consider donating to Toys for Tots. This incredible organization ensures that every child experiences the joy of Christmas. Visit their website to find a drop-off location near you.

articles.title: AASP/NJ Gather Automotive Community for Annual Meeting
articles.author: Jason Stahl

paras.en: The Alliance of Automotive Service Providers of New Jersey (AASP/NJ) recently gathered the automotive community for its annual meeting at Gran Centurions in Clark, N.J. The event recognized rising talent and standout shops, and also welcomed its youngest Hall of Fame inductee.
The evening opened with board of directors elections. Six members were reelected to three-year terms:
- Joe Amato Sr. (World Insurance Associates, Wall, N.J.)
- Dennis Cataldo Jr. (D&M Auto Body, Old Bridge, N.J.)
- Brad Crawford (Livingston Collision, Livingston, N.J.)
- Gary Gardella Jr. (County Line Auto Body, Howell, N.J.)
- Ted Rainer (Ocean Bay Auto Body, Point Pleasant, N.J.)

The spotlight then shifted to the industry’s next generation as Taina Rivera of Koplin Auto Body in Elizabeth, N.J., was recognized as the 2026 Russ Robson Memorial Scholarship recipient. Named for the former AASP/NJ president whose dedication to training helped shape young professionals, the annual scholarship recognizes an emerging talent who shows promise in the trade.
Petty Motorworks of Waretown, N.J., received the Mechanical Shop of the Year award, and Fantastic Plastic of Clifton, N.J., received the Stan Wilson/New Jersey Automotive Body Shop of the Year Award.
A milestone followed as Dennis Cataldo Jr. of D&M Auto Body in Old Bridge, N.J., was inducted into the AASP/NJ Hall of Fame, becoming the youngest recipient of the honor.
Comedian Danny Braff and TV and radio personality Robert Kelly (known for SiriusXM’s The Bonfire and his television and film appearances) delivered a comedy show for attendees.
For more information about AASP/NJ, visit aaspnj.org.

articles.title: Length of rental slightly up in Q3, shop scheduling backlogs down
articles.author: Lurah Lowery

paras.en: Enterprise Mobility reports that overall Length of Rental (LOR) for collision-related rentals in Q3 2026 was 15.5 days, up 0.4 days from Q2 and 0.1 days from Q3 2025.
“This modest rise is notable when comparing Q3 2025’s results to Q3 2024, when overall LOR declined 0.9 days; Q3 2026’s results are the first Q3-over-Q3 increase since 2022,” the report states.

“Apart from the early months of the pandemic in 2020, that was the highest percentage of shops reporting such an open schedule in the nearly 10 years since the quarterly “Who Pays” surveys began asking about scheduling backlog,” Yoswick said in the LOR report.
He added that work in progress (WIP) fell to another new low in Q3 2026, reaching 49% in September, according to CRASH Network’s “Collision Industry Business Perspectives” survey.
Ryan Mandell, Mitchell International’s vice president of strategy and market intelligence, added that the percentage of parts repaired continued upward in Q3, reaching 17.8% from 16.4% in Q3 2025.
Q3 drivable LOR was 14.6 days, a 0.2-day increase from Q3 2025. Alaska and Rhode Island had the joint-highest LOR at 18.9 days each, followed by Massachusetts at 16.8 days.
North Dakota had the lowest drivable LOR at 9.8 days, followed by Hawaii (11.2 days) and the District of Columbia (11.4 days).
Iowa recorded the largest increase, with drivable LOR up 1.7 days year over year to 12.9 days. Georgia (15.6 days) had the largest decrease, down 0.9 days.
Greg Horn, Chief Industry Relations Officer at PartsTrader, said drivable LOR “aligns closely with parts delivery days.”
Non-drivable LOR didn’t change compared to Q3 2025, remaining at 21.2 days.

Alaska had the highest non-drivable LOR at 30 days, followed by West Virginia at 26.3 days and Wyoming at 24.4 days. West Virginia (21.2 days) recorded its largest decrease, down 3.1 days from Q3 2025.

Total loss claim LOR was 14.2 days, a 0.3-day increase above Q3 2025. West Virginia had the highest total loss LOR at 18.1 days, followed by New Hampshire at 17.4 days and Rhode Island at 17.2 days. South Dakota had the lowest total loss LOR at 11.3 days.

“Total Loss frequency rose again to 21.0%, up from 20.3% in Q3 2025,” said Mandell in the report. “With more borderline vehicles ending up as write-offs, this contributes to some of the reduction in repairable claims volume the industry has been experiencing.”

According to JD Power’s 2026 U.S. Auto Claims Satisfaction Study, overall customer satisfaction decreases by 12 points (on a 1,000-point scale) due to total loss determinations, and increases by 4 points when damages are repairable.
Overall, the report found that 26% of auto insurance claims were classified as total losses in 2026, up from just 16% four years ago.
In the Q3 LOR report, Mandell adds that average first-party deductibles are declining, down to $809 in Q3 from $844 in Q3 2025.

“This may be an indicator that we are seeing more consumers switch insurance carriers as more competitive rates enter the ecosystem,” Mandell said. “This carrier switching is a catalyst for consumers to improve their coverage as they are able to attain a more favorable premium and thereby reduce their deductible or add back first-party coverages. Both of which are signs that we may see gradual increases in claims volumes in the near future.”
The Q3 Quarterly Insurance Signals Intelligence Report from JD Power and TransUnion shows auto insurance carrier switching increased even though year-over-year (YoY) shopping was flat.
The latest report shows shopping reached 13.2% and switching 5.1%, both up 0.6 percentage points from Q2.

A recent LexisNexis Risk Solutions whitepaper details survey findings on auto insurance shopping trends, stating that 72% of consumers who shopped for auto insurance are open to switching carriers. Of those, 17% said they were definitely seeking a new auto insurance company.
Featured image credit: dima_sidelnikov/iStock

articles.title: SCRS booth invites SEMA attendees to compete for ‘best welder’ and ‘best refinisher’
articles.author: Teresa Moss

paras.en: SEMA Show attendees are once again asked to compete in a virtual reality welding and refinishing competition to win prizes for their favorite automotive trade school at the Society of Collision Repair Specialists (SCRS) booth this week.

From Tuesday through Friday, visitors at the SCRS booth can take part in a fully immersive welding and refinishing competition powered by Skillveri’s virtual and mixed-reality training technology. The booth is located in the Upper South Hall, Booth #31147.
The competition will sort out the “best of the best” daily from 9:30–11:30 a.m. and 1–4:30 p.m. Winners will be announced via SCRS’s Facebook and LinkedIn pages Friday afternoon.

No pre-registration is needed, and it is open to students, instructors, and repair professionals. Participants can visit the SCRS booth during competition hours to compete in either the welding category, refinishing category, or both.
Attendees will compete for the titles of “Best Welder” and “Best Refinisher.” Finalists will receive a Full Series Pass to the 2027 SCRS Repairer Driven Education program at the SEMA Show.

Each winner will also select a U.S.-based automotive trade school to receive an equipment and training package made possible by Skillveri, Southern California Collision Equipment, Milwaukee Tool, and CAR-O-LINER.

- First Place Welding and Refinishing Finalists: Their selected school will receive a complete Skillveri virtual and mixed-reality training system, including a lifetime software license, VR headset, specialized welding or spray painting equipment, laptop, and supporting hardware.
- Second Place Welding Finalist: Their selected school will receive a Goliath Carts Weld Test Cart and Bench Mount Combo for welding.
- Second Place Refinish Finalists: Their selected school will receive a Goliath Carts Painters Toolbox.

- Third Place Finalists: Their selected schools will receive an extensive Milwaukee Tool equipment package featuring M12 and M18 FUEL cordless power tools, impact wrenches, ratchets, sanders, grinders, lighting, and specialty automotive repair equipment. The collection also includes extensive socket, wrench, and hand tool sets, along with a modular PACKOUT storage and organization system.
- Third Place Tie: CAR-O-LINER has provided a WEL32 MIG-MAG welding machine. If no third-place tie occurs, the welding machine will be added to the first-place welding award.
SCRS also recently announced that members now have flexible access to the Skillveri Chroma through an exclusive rental program.

The member benefit lets SCRS collision repair businesses evaluate new hires, run short-term training workshops, and build technician skills without the cost, mess, or material waste of live paint, an SCRS press release states.
Next door to the SCRS booth, Spanesi is also giving away $40,000 in prizes at Booth #31173.

Collision repair professionals visiting Spanesi Booth Nov. 3–6 can explore equipment and participate in an interactive experience focused on improving repair workflows and productivity, a Spanesi press release states.

“Spanesi Collision Course transforms a traditional booth visit into a hands-on experience where attendees can explore equipment, discover practical ways to improve repair processes in their own shops, and unlock prizes along the way,” according to the release.
Attendees scan a QR code on the show floor or at the booth to register. They then explore stations throughout the booth featuring measuring, structural repair, refinishing, and more.
“As participants visit stations, they’ll unlock a spin on a prize wheel featuring tools, industry-related gift cards, Spanesi merch, and other prizes,” the release states.

Participants who complete all stations qualify for six prize drawings, and one winner will receive a Touch V6 Portable measuring system valued at more than $40,000. Five additional winners will each receive $1,000 in Spanesi equipment credits. Winners will be selected in on-site drawings on Friday.

articles.title: Two-thirds of used car buyers concerned about undisclosed damage
articles.author: Teresa Moss

paras.en: Over two-thirds of used car buyers are concerned about hidden faults or undisclosed damage, according to a new United Kingdom survey completed by Cazoo Consumer Insight Panel.
Hidden faults or undisclosed damage was the largest concern identified in the survey of 2,025 buyers, according to Cazoo.

Overall, only around a third (35.5%) of used car buyers trust dealers and more than half expect friction as part of their buying experience, the survey found. Another 16.5% said they do not trust dealers and the remaining 48% are sitting on the fence.
Other concerns buyers have include an unclear vehicle history (45%), being overcharged (41%), and pushy sales tactics (36%).

Buyers said dealers could build trust by making a full vehicle history report available (61%), including independent vehicle inspections or warranties (42%), clear no-haggle pricing (42%), and verified customer reviews (40%).
Thirty-two percent of buyers said they value dealer accreditation from a trade body and 18% value photographs or videos of dealerships.

“Our latest Consumer Insight Panel identifies the role dealers can play in recognizing how trust can address the pain points experienced by many used car buyers,” Lucy Tugby, Cazoo chief marketing officer, says in the release. “Time and again we see how the best performing used car dealers are the ones with processes in place to ensure vehicles are described accurately and sold with independent inspections and warranties.”

Independent inspections of used vehicles is one suggestion the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) gives to consumers who are concerned their vehicles could have a counterfeit airbag.
NHTSA identified an 11th death caused by a specific banned counterfeit airbag part in September.

It is the first death involving one of the replacement airbag inflators installed in a Chevrolet Equinox, according to a NHTSA release. The previous 10 deaths and three serious injuries happened in Chevrolet Malibu and Hyundai Sonata vehicles.

Each deadly crash involved vehicles that had the original frontal driver airbag inflators replaced with a defective and likely illegally imported inflator marked with the identifier DTN60DB, the release states.

Teena Bohi, an Automotive Anti-Counterfeiting Council (A2C2) board member, said during a Collision Industry Conference (CIC) in July that NHTSA’s investigation has uncovered how dangerous counterfeit parts find their way into vehicles.
“Up until the point that a counterfeit product gets installed in the vehicle, everything about it is legal,” she added.
The vehicles are typically fleet vehicles or self-insured vehicles that were at some point totaled, Bohi said.

“The totaling of a vehicle isn’t a cut-and-dried process,” Bohi says. “The value is driven depending on whether it is self-insured, the state the vehicle was in, the insurer’s own practices, processes, and thresholds. There is a lot that goes into just determining if the vehicle is totaled.”

Next, the vehicle often goes to an auction. If it is a public auction, an airbag deployment will possibly be reported to the National Motor Vehicle Title Information System (NMVTIS). The system is a database meant to prevent the resale of stolen vehicles and track unsafe salvage cars. If the vehicle goes to a wholesale or private auction, the previous crash information is not always captured, she said.
After the repair, vehicles are retitled, and the process can vary state to state, including the inspection process, Bohi says. Many don’t require airbag inspections.
“There are a lot of gaps where attention could be focused that could help address these types of issues,” Bohi said.

NHTSA “urges” owners of used vehicles that have previously been in a crash since 2020 to have their vehicles inspected. It also “urges” used vehicle owners and buyers to learn their vehicle’s history and ensure it has genuine airbag inflators.

“If a vehicle has been in a previous crash where the air bag deployed, it should be inspected by a reputable mechanic immediately to ensure the air bag is a legitimate replacement equivalent to the original,” NHTSA says in the release. “Owners should not attempt to inspect their air bag themselves. If a vehicle is found to have a DTN60DB inflator, it should not be driven until the inflator is replaced with genuine parts.”

Technicians looking for guidance on identifying a DTN airbag can also refer to an NHTSA document. The document outlines the materials and design characteristics that can be used to indicate whether an airbag is a counterfeit. DTN airbags are also often marked with DTN60DB. Yet, it can be hard to identify DTN airbags when they’re still installed in a vehicle.
Bohi said the council has reached out to the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) and the Department of Transportation (DOT) to get clarification on those processes.

“How do you safely handle these things, and what do you do if you get one? Because there are special permits to transport or get rid of these things if there is a counterfeit because we don’t know what’s in them. It’s an unknown explosive, potentially,” Bohi said.

NHTSA’s technician guidance does offer warnings that strongly advise technicians not to electronically probe or electrify airbag connecting terminals because they can detonate and cause serious injury or death.

Bud Center, I-CAR director of technical products and curriculum, previously told Repairer Driven News that electronic probes can be used to deploy a removed airbag. However, if a repairer believes an airbag is counterfeit, they should contact the vehicle’s OEM and ask for instructions.
“You want to make sure you are not going to deploy something that is unsafe,” Center said.
Center dives into the issue of counterfeit parts from the collision shop level in an I-CAR Repairers Realm series.
Nearly all OEMs and many major aftermarket parts companies have people within their organizations who can answer questions concerning products, Bohi said.

If an owner has a vehicle with one of these suspect inflators, they should contact their local Homeland Security Investigations office or FBI field office to report it or submit an online complaint to the National Intellectual Property Rights Coordination Center.
Owners should also contact NHTSA online or by calling the agency’s Vehicle Safety Hotline at 888-327-4236, Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. Eastern time.

articles.title: Corey Bartlett Wins AWDA’s Excellence in Education Award
articles.author: Doug Kaufman

paras.en: The Aftermarket Warehouse Distributors Association (AWDA), a community of the Auto Care Association, presented the 2026 Art Fisher Award for Excellence in Education, to Corey Bartlett, CEO of Auto Parts Headquarters (APH) based in St. Cloud, MN. The award was presented on November 1st by AWDA Vice Chair Young Suhr at AWDA’s 2026 Annual Conference in Las Vegas.

AWDA’s Art Fisher Award for Excellence in Education is presented annually to an aftermarket company or individual that demonstrates outstanding commitment to education and training, either within their organization or throughout the industry. Given in memory of former AWDA Chairman Art Fisher, the award grants scholarships in the name of the award winner to two students enrolled in the automotive aftermarket management program at Northwood University.

Corey Bartlett has shown a unique interest in education from the day he began working professionally for APH. Within his first ten years, he reorganized staff and increased training for employees. Leading by example, he himself completed the University of the Aftermarket’s Leadership 2010 at Ohio State University, and he earned his AAP and MAAP designations at the University of the Aftermarket in 2002 and 2009 respectively.

“Corey has shown incredible initiative in supporting training and continuing education,” said John R. Washbish, president and CEO of the Aftermarket Auto Parts Alliance, Inc. “Through his leadership roles and example, he has consistently improved the education and standards of his staff, the Alliance, and the industry as a whole.”

Now as CEO, Bartlett primarily oversees the operations of the business and has continued to emphasize education. As the company expanded to include medium, heavy duty, and agricultural aspects, Bartlett and his managers developed a 101 class to further educate his staff about the new aspects of the business. He partnered with a local technical college to provide hands-on experience, and the company saw nearly 100% participation among its 1,200 employees.
While serving as board liaison of the Alliance’s Sales & Marketing Committee, Bartlett oversaw the group’s scholarship program and helped create the Technician of the Year program.

Outside of the Alliance and APH, Bartlett has chaired the Automotive Warehouse Distributors Association (AWDA) Board of Governors, serves as a mentor for the Young Auto Care Networking Group (YANG), and has been a generous supporter and active proponent of the Auto Care Political Action Committee since 2015. He was named the AWDA Pursuit of Excellence honoree in 2017.

Bartlett is involved in his local community, enthusiastically supporting WACOSA – a nonprofit organization that helps adults with disabilities connect with local businesses – through Chili Cook Off efforts with his father, and opening up APH facilities for use by local nonprofits.

articles.title: How the Alignment Process is Changing
articles.author: Andrew Markel

paras.en: For technicians working in an alignment pit before the 1980s, obtaining the initial angles was a relatively easy process because most vehicles had steel wheels. Mounting the alignment “sensor” with rim clamps provided a very accurate representation of the front wheels’ planes of rotation for measuring camber, caster and toe. However, because the tools used to measure these angles were contained inside the sensor head, they were very fragile and frequently fell out of calibration.

By the 1980s, more vehicles were being equipped with cast-alloy wheels that did not have a suitable lip for mounting the sensor head. Getting a secure grip on the rim became more difficult. It was not uncommon for a rim clamp to come off during an alignment and damage the expensive head.

In the 1990s, alignment technology began to change with improvements in digital cameras. Engineers started mounting cameras to fixtures positioned in front of the vehicle. The expensive sensors at the wheels were replaced with simple targets that the cameras could scan to determine the alignment angles.
However, cameras added a new wrinkle to the alignment process: the rolling-compensation procedure. This procedure also helped resolve problems caused by attaching alignment targets to alloy wheels.

Nearly every modern chassis alignment system uses this step to obtain accurate alignment measurements. First, the vehicle is positioned 12 to 20 inches behind the front turntables. Most systems require the targets to be attached so that a specified part of each target is level with the center of the wheel. The vehicle is then rolled forward onto the turntables. This process is called rolling compensation.
Modern camera-based aligners attach a target to each wheel, and the vehicle is rolled backward or forward a short distance while the cameras track each target through part of a wheel revolution.

As the wheel rotates, the aligner observes the path traveled by the target. The system detects changes in the target’s orientation or the center of the wheel’s rotation caused by clamp runout, wheel damage or an off-center target. From these observations, the software calculates the relationship between the target and the wheel’s actual plane of rotation. This prevents a slightly crooked clamp or target from being interpreted as camber or toe.

The primary purpose of rolling compensation is to establish the true rotational plane and centerline of each wheel while compensating for target or clamp mounting errors. Camber and toe can then be calculated directly. Caster and steering-axis inclination require a separate steering sweep.

Some systems do not require rolling compensation. These systems typically use lasers, mirrors or other devices mounted near the center of the lift to calculate the alignment angles. On some heavy-duty alignment systems, the target or sensor is mounted directly to the spindle.
With today’s electronic parking brakes and advanced driver-assistance systems, including collision-mitigation systems, the alignment process is becoming more challenging.

Even pulling a vehicle onto an alignment rack can be a struggle. We recently had a 2024 Audi Q4 come into our training center. As the technician began driving the vehicle onto the ramps of the drive-on lift, the car applied the brakes, stopped and displayed a collision warning on the instrument panel. The technician applied the accelerator, and the vehicle eventually began moving again.

Even after reviewing the service information, it was unclear what caused this behavior. Was the alignment equipment interfering with the vehicle’s sensors, or was the system reacting to the proximity of the wall and toolbox in front of the vehicle? Were the lasers on the cameras causing the issue?

We had a similar incident with a 2023 Ford F-150 that bucked like a bronco (not a Ford Bronco) while we were positioning it on a drive-on lift. Once again, neither the service information nor the owner’s manual clearly explained the behavior.

Most other late-model vehicles with collision-mitigation systems that we have driven onto the same lift issue audible and visual warnings when they detect what they interpret as a possible threat in the bay. However, they rarely intervene and stop the vehicle.

Even more challenging are the procedures for preparing a vehicle for an alignment when it must be moved during rolling compensation. The primary difficulties involve keeping the parking brake released and the transmission in neutral.

Many modern vehicles use electronic parking brakes that engage automatically when the vehicle is parked. Some systems do this for safety, while others use the parking brake to prevent slight vehicle movement before the transmission’s parking pawl fully engages.
Even if the transmission is placed in neutral and the ignition is switched off using a push button or physical key, the parking brake may engage automatically without any action from the driver.

On many vehicles, the driver’s gear selection does not have final authority. Even after neutral is selected, a control module may shift the transmission into park when it detects certain conditions, such as an open driver’s door or an unbuckled seat belt.

Modern transmissions use electronic driver interfaces and communicate with numerous other vehicle systems. This integration has made selecting neutral—and keeping the transmission in neutral—more challenging.

Working around systems designed to protect the driver requires awareness, accurate information and, in some cases, a scan tool. Many vehicles have built-in procedures or operating modes that allow them to remain in neutral and roll freely. The challenge is finding the correct procedure.

Many late-model Ford vehicles have a Stay in Neutral or Temporary Neutral mode that remains active for a limited period. Depending on the vehicle, the mode may be engaged by holding the brake pedal, selecting neutral and pressing the manual-mode or low-range button when prompted.

Some Tesla alignment procedures require the technician to buckle the front seat belts and manually close the front door latches before placing the vehicle in neutral. This prevents the vehicle from determining that the occupants have exited and automatically applying park or the electronic parking brake.

Other vehicles allow technicians to activate these modes through the infotainment system. Some require a particular sequence of button presses to keep the transmission in neutral and the electronic parking brake released. Instructions for these procedures may be found in the service information or owner’s manual.

In other cases, a scan tool with bidirectional controls or dedicated service functions may be needed to select neutral, place the braking system in a service mode or release the electronic parking brake. Regardless of the method, technicians must follow the manufacturer’s instructions and use wheel chocks whenever the vehicle is not being moved for the rolling-compensation procedure.

It is easy to see that alignment and ADAS calibration are beginning to merge into a single service as chassis alignment and ADAS sensor positioning become increasingly dependent on each other. One area that is currently growing is the integration of vehicle communication capabilities into the alignment and calibration bay. As more late-model vehicles come out of warranty, alignment service will require an even more increased use of scan tools to initiate adjustments and calibrations.

articles.title: MEYLE to Bring Back Scholarship Fundraiser at AAPEX 2026
articles.author: Alex Crissey

paras.en: MEYLE announced that it will bring its German license plate fundraiser to raise money for Northwood University scholarships back to AAPEX 2026 (Nov. 3-5 in Las Vegas).

MEYLE will host the fundraiser at its exhibit at the show, featuring a German license plate stamping machine. Visitors can create custom MEYLE-branded plates in exchange for donations benefiting Northwood students.
Last year’s initiative generated $9,171 in donations. MEYLE supplemented that amount with a $5,000 matching contribution, bringing the total to $14,171.
Northwood Student Receives First MEYLE Scholarship

Earlier this year, Quinn Balcam became the first recipient of the MEYLE scholarship. Balcam, an automotive aftermarket management major from Bloomington, Indiana, serves as president of Northwood’s student aftermarket club.

MEYLE notes that Balcam has demonstrated his industry commitment through multiple internships and leadership in the Northwood University International Auto Show’s aftermarket division. He has also participated in events including AAPEX, SEMA and Heavy-Duty Aftermarket Week.

“Seeing the funds raised at AAPEX translate into scholarship support for a student like Quinn illustrates why partnerships like this are so important,” said James O’Dell, director of aftermarket education at Northwood University. “The automotive aftermarket needs talented, motivated young professionals, and MEYLE is helping our students gain both the financial support and industry connections they need to succeed.”

articles.title: The Effect of Thin Brake Fluid on Vehicle Systems
articles.author: Christian Hinton

paras.en: Lower-viscosity brake fluid plays a growing role in modern brake systems. Today’s vehicles require brake fluid to move quickly through hydraulic control units that support ABS, stability control, traction control and several ADAS braking functions.
Modern brake systems use faster valves, tighter internal passages and more frequent automatic brake interventions than systems used 20 years ago.

As a result, many late-model vehicles require lower-viscosity brake fluid. The goal is to maintain efficient fluid movement at low temperatures so the hydraulic unit can build and release pressure quickly.
Lower-Viscosity Brake Fluid Supports Faster Response

The ABS hydraulic unit is used, not only during panic stops, but for electronic stability control, traction control, adaptive cruise control, collision mitigation braking and automatic emergency braking.

Inside the hydraulic control unit, brake fluid moves through small valves and narrow passages. Lower viscosity allows pressure to increase and decrease faster, helping the system make quicker and more precise braking corrections.
Brake fluid condition is also important. Moisture contamination can increase viscosity, lower the boiling point and raise corrosion risk.
Technicians should use the exact brake fluid specified by the vehicle manufacturer and replace it according to the proper service information.

articles.title: Dipstick Replacement Sensors: How They Work
articles.author: Andrew Markel

paras.en: GM has taken a lot of guff recently for eliminating the dipstick on some of their newer V8 engines and replacing it with a sensor. Let’s talk about how those sensors actually work, and how and when they measure the oil level.

It’s not like, for example, a brake master cylinder that has a float and a level that turns on the light on the dash when it reaches a certain level. These sensors are ultrasonic. In other words, it’s sending out a sound wave into the oil pan and determining the oil level that way.

How does it know when to measure the level of oil in the oil pan? If you’re using a dipstick, the vehicle would be parked, it probably wouldn’t be running, and that’s when you’re checking the oil level. The sensor works the same way: It’s only measuring the oil level at certain instances. Let’s say it’s in Park when you first start up. Let’s say you’re sitting at a traffic light; that is when it’s measuring the level.
For more on sensors and how they work, including oxygen and TPMS sensors, watch the video above.

articles.title: Bennie Skelton Named 2026 WIX Filters Counter Professional of the Year
articles.author: Jason Morgan

paras.en: WIX Filters and Counterman have named Bennie Skelton of Crow-Burlingame’s Bumper to Bumper store in Neosho, Missouri, the 2026 Counter Professional of the Year. Skelton brings more than four decades of parts experience to the counter, building customer relationships that now extend across generations. His career reflects a commitment to helping customers and a determination to overcome challenges.

Skelton entered the parts field in 1980 when he enlisted in the U.S. Air Force. During 12 years of service, he learned to identify parts using microfiche and paper catalogs, measure engine components and supervise military and civilian personnel. While stationed in California, he worked weekends at an auto parts story after leaving the Air Force in 1992. Skelton joined Crow-Burlingame in 2009.

“Bennie has great customer service and has a lifetime of knowledge,” said Darren Brewer, manager of the Neosho store. “I don’t have to tell him to do something when he sees it needs to be done, he does it. He’s the best man I’ve ever worked with. ”
Brewer credits Skelton with helping strengthen the store’s financial performance and praised his initiative, sales ability and perseverance.

In 2012, Skelton suffered a major stroke that affected his speech and the use of his right side. He spent months relearning how to walk and talk, adapting to perform tasks left-handed. Today, he continues building hydraulic hoses, pulling parts and completing paperwork while serving the customers he knows so well.

articles.title: Schwartz Advisors’ Cruickshank Named CAWA Vice Chairman
articles.author: Jeff White

paras.en: Schwartz Advisors partner Brian Cruickshank took the oath of office as vice chairman of the California Automotive Wholesalers’ Association (CAWA). (secretary). Dan Hanson Jr., Blue Streak Electronics, serves as immediate past chair.

During his three-decade career in the motor vehicle aftermarket, Cruickshank has held numerous volunteer leadership positions. He has served on committees within the Auto Care Association and the Automotive Warehouse Distributors Association (AWDA) Board of Governors. His involvement also includes the University of the Aftermarket Foundation and other industry organizations.

“Brian’s involvement with CAWA reflects our firm’s ongoing commitment to giving back to the industry while keeping a close pulse on the issues and trends shaping the motor vehicle aftermarket,” said SA managing partner Rick Schwartz, who also serves on the Auto Care Association Board of Directors.

articles.title: Advance Auto Parts Opens First Store in Richboro, Pa.
articles.author: Mary DellaValle

paras.en: Advance Auto Parts opened its first store in Richboro on October 29, expanding access to parts, tools and expertise for local drivers and automotive professionals. The company marked the opening of the store at 1039 2nd Street Pike with a ribbon-cutting ceremony alongside local officials and representatives from Middle Bucks Institute of Technology who were on site to accept a donation for the school’s automotive technology program.

The donation will help students gain hands-on experience, training, and career opportunities through the school’s automotive technology programs. Skilled automotive technicians continue to be in high demand, with approximately 70,000 openings projected annually through 2034, according to U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.

“Opening our first store in Richboro is an exciting milestone for our team,” said Eli Rosa, regional vice president, Advance Auto Parts. “We’re grateful for the opportunity to serve this community and proud to support students at Middle Bucks Institute of Technology as they pursue hands-on learning and explore careers in the automotive field.”

“We appreciate Advance Auto Parts‘ support of our automotive technology program,” said Dr. Mark Covelle, administrative director at Middle Bucks Institute of Technology. “Donations like this help support hands-on learning opportunities for our students as they build skills and prepare for future careers in the industry.”

articles.title: Scientists find the best evidence yet of potentially habitable volcanic vents on Mars
articles.author: Elizabeth Howell

paras.en: A noxious gas found seeping through cracks on Mars hints that there may be magma flowing beneath the Red Planet's surface — and perhaps even an environment similar to habitable ones on Earth, a new study suggests.

Europe's ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) spacecraft spotted a possible signal of hydrogen chloride gas leaking from rifts in the region of Alba Mons, the largest volcano on Mars in terms of surface area. (Mars' famous Olympus Mons is the largest volcano in terms of height.) Scientists interpret this gas as emissions from hot magma below the regolith of Mars.

Although more research is required to confirm the emissions, the team suggested that Alba Mons may host an environment similar to hydrothermal vents on Earth, where life once likely arose and continues to thrive today.

The study, published in the journal Science Advances Wednesday (Nov. 4), is not the first to suggest that magma may be flowing on Mars; NASA's InSight lander interpreted its presence through seismic observations and modeling earlier this year. But the new findings are the strongest evidence yet of gases being released by dormant volcanoes on Mars, first study author Alexander Trokhimovskiy, at Russia's Space Research Institute, told Live Science.

"Our study offers a complementary and potentially independent line of evidence [of Martian magma]: Atmospheric observations that reveal a possible signature of gas release from a subsurface magmatic system," Trokhimovskiy wrote in an email.

TGO first detected hydrogen chloride gas in Mars' atmosphere in 2021, but scientists were hesitant to link it to volcanic activity. The gas appeared to be seasonal, its distribution was not localized at a possible volcanic region, and other signs of volcanic gases, like sulfur, were not present, study co-author Kevin Olson, a visiting researcher at the University of Oxford who studies Mars gases, told Live Science in a separate email.
Further work, however, suggested that the gas wasn't just popping up in the warmer spring and summer in Mars' southern hemisphere; it also appeared in the winter in the northern hemisphere, he noted.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"I managed to catch two observations from the start of northern winter in the first Mars year of our mission, and a single observation the next year," Olson said, adding that a year on Mars is closer to two years on Earth due to the planet's wider orbit. "These out-of-season measurements were close to one another in location and time in both years, which was rather surprising. We then set about creating a campaign of special, targeted measurements at this time and place."

That campaign lasted two Mars years — roughly four Earth years — and increased the likelihood that scientists are seeing "an injection" of hydrogen chloride into the atmosphere from volcano-adjacent vents, Olson said.

The scientists confirmed the unseasonal observations in the northern hemisphere, finding a "distinct and pronounced signal" that then diminishes and falls below the spacecraft's detection threshold. "This inconsistency is more suggestive of a puff of gas entering the atmosphere than of regular atmospheric chemistry," he said. "While the link remains a hypothesis, we have now seen this gas appear locally, and nowhere else, over four Mars years of observations."
- Gargantuan volcano on Mars found hidden 'in plain sight,' and it could hold potential signs of life
- An anomaly in Mars' mantle could trigger volcanoes to erupt — and may be causing the whole planet to spin faster
- Grand Canyon-size 'scar' on Mars revealed like never before in striking new satellite photos

Daniel Mège, also a co-author of the paper and a professor who studies planetary geology at the Polish Academy of Sciences, identified the fissures where the gas may be emerging. He said the complementary evidence from InSight (on the ground) and TGO (circling above) helps give the study weight: InSight spotted activity in the crust, while TGO detected the emissions in the atmosphere.

Although magma activity is not in itself a sign of life, Mège noted that Earth's first life-forms came from sites like hydrothermal zones, which have a similar confluence of materials and energy as the potential vents on Mars. But conditions would need to be favorable in that area for at least millions of years to allow life to form, he cautioned.

"If these requirements are met at local scale, at the scale of the seepage structures, then living organisms might wait for us to discover them," he told Live Science in an email. "But maintaining stable conditions over such a long period at a very local scale is not obvious."

Elizabeth Howell was staff reporter at Space.com between 2022 and 2024 and a regular contributor to Live Science and Space.com between 2012 and 2022. Elizabeth's reporting includes multiple exclusives with the White House, speaking several times with the International Space Station, witnessing five human spaceflight launches on two continents, flying parabolic, working inside a spacesuit, and participating in a simulated Mars mission. Her latest book, "Why Am I Taller?" (ECW Press, 2022) is co-written with astronaut Dave Williams.

articles.title: Colorful 1,800-year-old belt buckle discovered in a Ukrainian forest may have belonged to a nomadic equestrian warrior
articles.author: Kristina Killgrove

paras.en: Archaeologists in Ukraine have found a colorful belt buckle that may have been worn by a nomadic equestrian warrior 1,800 years ago on the fringes of the Roman Empire.

The belt buckle was unearthed by local residents in the Tsetsyn Forest in southeastern Ukraine and given to Antonii Moisei, a professor at Bukovinian State Medical University, according to a translated statement. The roughly square metal buckle, which is about 0.8 inches (2.1 centimeters) on each side, has teal, blue and yellow enamel decorations.

The style of the decoration and the metal construction place the creation of the buckle in the second to third centuries A.D., when this part of Ukraine was in the ancient province of Roman Dacia, according to Moisei.

Under Emperor Trajan, Rome fought the Dacian Wars (A.D. 101-102 and 105-106) against the denizens of the Dacian kingdom and its leader, Decebalus. Roman legions destroyed Dacia and annexed it as a new province. Trajan celebrated his victory in Rome, complete with a famous column that depicts details of the Dacian Wars.

In addition to the buckle, Moisei collected a decorative belt fitting and three small, round metal objects that probably belonged to the same belt. Moisei created a reconstruction of what the belt might have looked like before it was lost in the forest nearly two millennia ago.

But it's unclear who lost the belt. One of Moisei's theories is that the belt belonged to a horse-riding Sarmatian warrior originally from the Black Sea region. The Sarmatians were a group of tribes that lived outside the borders of the Roman Empire, in what are now central Ukraine, southern Russia and the Balkans. While some Sarmatian warriors fought against the incursion of the Roman Empire, others fought with Rome as mercenaries.

The metal belt fragments are part of a Roman provincial craft tradition, according to the statement, and they may have been obtained through trade or as a trophy of war. But Moisei is still studying the artifacts to confirm whether they were Sarmatian. Either way, the military belt provides new evidence of Roman military contact on the outskirts of the empire, and future work could help experts understand how the Romans interacted with the local Dacians during wartime.
From Augustus to Nero, see how much you know about ancient Rome's famous leaders with our Roman emperor quiz!

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

articles.title: Swift has fallen: NASA's 22-year-old space telescope burns up over Sumatra
articles.author: Kenna Hughes-Castleberry

paras.en: It's the end of an era: NASA's Swift telescope has reached the conclusion of its nearly 22-year mission, burning up in Earth's atmosphere after studying some of the universe's most powerful and mysterious events.

According to NASA, the spacecraft reentered the atmosphere at "7:39 a.m. EST Wednesday over the North Sumatra region of Indonesia, at approximately 3.4 degrees north latitude and 98.6 degrees east longitude." NASA expected most of the telescope's structure to burn up during its passage through Earth's atmosphere, estimating a 1-in-2,100 chance of any surviving debris falling over a populated area. No damage or injuries have been reported.

Weighing approximately 3,200 pounds (1,450 kilograms), the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory was initially designed for a two-year mission, but it far exceeded expectations. Over two decades, Swift became an important tool in the study of gamma-ray bursts, supernovas, black holes and other cosmic phenomena.

Launched in November 2004, Swift was designed to detect gamma-ray bursts, powerful explosions that occur throughout the universe. Its three onboard telescopes let scientists observe cosmic events across different wavelengths, including ultraviolet, optical and X-ray light. The telescope could swivel to focus on different sky targets in a matter of minutes, allowing it to rapidly follow up on sudden events like supernova explosions.
NASA estimates that Swift's scientific observations have contributed to approximately 7,000 research papers, leaving behind an extensive collection that scientists can continue studying for years.
- Gamma-ray bursts reveal largest structure in the universe is bigger and closer to Earth than we knew: 'The jury is still out on what it all means.'
- Did a NASA telescope really 'see' dark matter? Strange gamma-rays spark bold claims, but scientists urge caution
- Brightest gamma-ray burst ever detected defies explanation

Swift's return was driven by atmospheric drag, which eventually slowed the spacecraft and caused its orbit to decay. Increased solar activity intensified the drag, thus accelerating the space telescope's descent toward Earth.

Earlier this year, NASA explored an ambitious rescue mission to extend Swift's operational life. In August 2026, a privately developed robotic spacecraft built by Katalyst Space Technologies was intended to rendezvous with Swift and boost it into a higher orbit. However, the mission failed after launching, leaving the observatory on its path toward reentry.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

NASA officially ended Swift's scientific operations on Oct. 20 after its declining altitude made observations too difficult. For NASA and the broader astronomy community, Swift's story is a reminder that even missions designed to last just a few years can fundamentally change our understanding of our universe.

Kenna Hughes-Castleberry is the Content Manager at Live Science. Formerly, she was the Content Manager at Space.com and before that the Science Communicator at JILA, a physics research institute. Kenna is also a book author, with her upcoming book 'Octopus X' scheduled for release in spring of 2027. Her beats include physics, health, environmental science, technology, AI, animal intelligence, corvids, and cephalopods.

articles.title: Forensic Analysis of Frozen Inca Mummies Reveals That Sacrificed Children Were Plied With Coca Leaves, Corn Beer and Ayahuasca Compounds Before Death

paras.en: The capacocha was one of the most sacred ceremonies of the Inca Empire, involving the sacrifice of children on the high-altitude volcanic peaks of the Andes. Now, new research reveals how children were drugged in preparation for their fate.

Researchers analyzed hair and fingernail samples taken from eight frozen child mummies discovered on mountains across Peru and Argentina: one boy and seven girls who were between the ages of six and 14 when they died some five centuries ago. The toxicological screenings revealed that the youths were administered intoxicating and mind-altering substances including cocaine, ceremonial corn beer and an alkaloid linked to ayahuasca brews, according to a study published in Antiquity this week.

While earlier studies primarily focused on coca leaves, Dagmara Socha, a bioarchaeologist at the University of Warsaw and the study’s first author, explains in a statement, “our aim was to identify a broader range of psychoactive substances administered to the children and to determine whether patterns in their use could provide new insights into how capacocha ceremonies were conducted at different locations.”
“Recent advances in toxicology now allow for the identification of low concentrations of such substances,” she adds.

Early Spanish chroniclers like friar Martín de Murúa noted that capacocha ceremonies were meant to ensure there would be “no famine nor lack of fruits of the earth, nor would there be drought, nor pestilence, nor rebellion.” But how priests managed the victims’ emotional and physical states remained poorly understood.

Inca rulers sacrificed healthy young boys and girls from across the vast empire during moments of profound crisis like prolonged droughts, famines or political turmoil to appease the mountain deities and restore cosmic order. Rather than viewing these victims as mere casualties, the Inca considered the children to be sacred ambassadors destined to ascend as eternal messengers between humanity and the gods.

“The ritual also had a political dimension, helping the Inca state establish relationships with local communities and incorporate regional deities into the imperial religious system,” Socha tells Gizmodo’s Gayoung Lee.
“Being selected for capacocha was an extraordinary honor that elevated not only the social status of the children but also that of their entire families,” she tells Discover’s Anastasia Scott.

Because chemicals become locked in the keratin protein of growing hair and nails, they preserve a record of an individual’s final months alive. Using sensitive modern forensic techniques, the team detected cocaine in all eight mummies, confirming that each child chewed coca leaves, a plant held sacred by the Inca. Figurines buried alongside the mummies also feature prominent bulges in their cheeks, representing coca quids. Besides a ceremonial importance, the coca leaves likely helped suppress hunger, relieved exhaustion and counteracted severe altitude sickness during the victims’ ascents to the mountaintop sacrificial sites.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Four of the victims also showed chemical signs of alcohol consumption. This likely came from chicha, a fermented maize beer that was given to the children to dull their senses and calm them as the sacrifice neared, per the statement. Chicha residue was also discovered in vessels interred with the mummies.

“What is interesting is that, although coca appears to have been a common element of the capacocha ritual, the use of other psychoactive substances varied between individuals and locations,” Socha tells Gizmodo. “This suggests that the preparation of children for sacrifice was not uniform across the Inca Empire.”

Among the mummies examined was the famous “Lady of Ampato,” popularly known as Juanita, an adolescent girl discovered on Ampato, a Peruvian stratovolcano, in 1995. In her fingernails, researchers identified traces of harmine, an active alkaloid derived from a vine that is one of the foundational ingredients of ayahuasca. Because harmine possesses notable antidepressant properties, researchers believe it was administered specifically to elevate her spirits, ease her fear and attune her senses.
Researchers identified traces of cocaine use in the brain tissue of two people buried in Italy in the 1600s. It was previously thought to have spread to Europe only in the 19th century.

Since the vine only grows in the Amazon rainforest and had to travel hundreds of miles over trade networks to reach the sacrifice sites in the Andes, it shows that ensuring “emotional wellbeing and positive mood of the children, who were regarded as messengers to the gods, may have been an important part of the ceremony,” Socha tells Discover.

The chronological record in hair strands allowed the team to map out how ritual preparations intensified over time. For an eight-year-old girl found on Mount Chuscha in Argentina, chemical markers revealed that her coca intake climbed over six months, while signs of alcohol appeared exclusively during her final weeks, signaling a transition into the final ceremonial stage.

“We cannot reconstruct the children’s emotions or determine precisely how they experienced these events,” Socha tells New Scientist’s James Woodford. “However, we should not assume that being selected for a prestigious religious ceremony necessarily meant that the experience was not frightening or traumatic.”

articles.title: Actually, You Can Go Back to Constantinople. A Landmark Exhibition Reconstructs the Imperial City With 1,600 Years of Treasures From Byzantine and Ottoman Times

paras.en: Napoleon Bonaparte once supposedly declared Constantinople to be “the empire of the world.” From its founding as the capital of the Byzantine Empire under Roman emperor Constantine in the 4th century C.E. until the fall of the Ottoman Empire in the 1920s, the city today known as Istanbul was indeed the epicenter of two successive, world-defining civilizations.

The city’s role in that sweeping, nearly 1,600-year saga is the focus of “Constantinople to Istanbul: One City, Two Empires,” a major exhibition at London’s Victoria and Albert Museum. Opening November 7, the exhibition unites more than 200 rare objects from Byzantine and Ottoman times.
“Creating this exhibition has been an exciting adventure, bringing together two worlds that are usually kept well apart,” Tim Stanley, the exhibition’s curator, says in a statement.

“The artistic ideas generated there in its double history as an imperial capital still play a major role in the world,” he adds. “By combining the stories of these two empires and the amazing art they both produced, we have been able to release the stories of Constantinople and Istanbul from their separate boxes and let them enjoy the limelight together.”

The exhibition unfolds across four chronological sections: “Roman Beginnings,” charting the city’s imperial origins; “Heaven and Earth,” exploring monumental sacred architecture; “A Capital Reborn,” examining the Ottoman imperial court’s role in artmaking; and “Life in the City,” capturing the vibrant, multi-ethnic metropolis of the 19th century.

The journey begins in 330 C.E., when Constantine selected the former Greek settlement of Byzantium as an eastern counterpart to Rome. Among the early relics is a bronze serpent head from the famous Serpent Column, which Constantine relocated directly from Delphi to furnish the city’s central hippodrome.

At the hippodrome, Romans “thronged in their thousands to cheer on the chariot racers and wolf whistle dancing girls as they performed lascivious burlesques,” Peter Sarris, a historian at the University of Cambridge, writes in the London Times. One such dancer, Sarris points out, was Theodora, the future wife of the Byzantine emperor Justinian.

In the sixth century, Justinian commissioned the Hagia Sophia, a spellbindingly large cathedral that was built in less than six years and served as the religious core of the East Roman world. When envoys sent by Vladimir the Great, the pagan Grand Prince of Kyiv, visited the Hagia Sophia in the 10th century, they were so mesmerized by its grandeur that they “knew not whether [they] were in heaven or earth.”

The exhibition assembles a “rich range of liturgical objects” from the cathedral and beyond, per the statement. One rare object on view is the Lincoln Typikon, an illuminated, 14th-century manuscript from a Constantinople nunnery, on loan from Lincoln College, Oxford, for the first time in six decades, the Art Newspaper’s Gareth Harris reports. The typikon’s delicate illustrations of the convent of the Virgin of Sure Hope offer a vivid window into monastic life just a century before the capital’s fall.

paras.en: After the Ottomans conquered Constantinople in 1453, the city’s new rulers both honored and transformed their new domain. Sultan Mehmet II converted Hagia Sophia into a mosque while intentionally retaining its original name, turning the ancient Christian monument into the aesthetic blueprint for grand Islamic architecture across the capital.
- The Byzantine Empire used religious art, such as portable icons and jeweled reliquaries, to bolster geopolitical alliances.

- One standout example is Saint Lawrence’s Pallium, a lavish 13th-century silk depiction of the patron saint of Genoa guiding Byzantine emperor Michael VIII into a strategic pact with the Genoese. Michael gifted the Genoese this cloth to seal the deal.

The transition to Ottoman splendor is heralded by Gentile Bellini’s 1480 portrait of Mehmet II, reflecting a court hungry for Renaissance artistry. The later imperial rooms showcase opulent displays of secular and military authority. Among them are a 30-foot-long, 17th-century processional scroll illustrating the sultan’s elaborate palace retinue, a silk kaftan woven with shimmering gold thread and a pair of gold pistols presented by the Ottoman court to Britain’s King George III, per the Telegraph’s Alastair Sooke.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The exhibition concludes away from royal palaces, diving into the lively social spaces of the 19th-century city of Istanbul through depictions of buzzing coffee houses, literary salons and public bathhouses.
“This is a sumptuous voyage to Byzantium via Istanbul,” Jonathan Jones writes for the Guardian. “Linger in the baths, in your tall wooden shoes and silk towel, and enjoy the artifice of eternity.”
“Constantinople to Istanbul: One City, Two Empires” is on view at the V&A South Kensington in London from November 7, 2026, to May 9, 2027.

articles.title: It's Not Just You: Some Fast-Flying Birds Also Get Jet Lag

paras.en: Traveling rapidly across multiple time zones often throws our internal clocks out of whack. But new research suggests jet lag is not unique to humans—some birds may also experience it.

A new study published October 29 in the journal Science finds that the internal clocks of Manx shearwaters can get out of sync with local time because the birds fly so fast. These jet lag-like time shifts confuse their sun-based compasses, and cause them to become slightly disoriented and fly a little off course.

Black on top and white on bottom, Manx shearwaters are medium-sized seabirds that spend most of their lives flapping over the open ocean. But in late winter and early spring, roughly 80 percent of the world’s population returns to the steep, grassy islands off the western coasts of the United Kingdom to breed. Here, they reunite with their lifelong mates and nest in underground burrows, with females laying one egg that eventually hatches into a fluffy chick.

Adult birds head out in search of food, bringing back tasty morsels of herring, sardine and sprat to feed their growing chicks. The birds that nest near the U.K. regularly travel more than 600 miles west from their breeding islands to forage in the food-rich waters of the Irish Sea and the northeast Atlantic Ocean. Once they’ve filled their bellies, they make the return eastward journey, navigating back to their colonies with “remarkable efficiency,” the study’s co-authors write in the paper.
Shearwater chicks are so well-fed by their parents that they become too big to leave the nest. They often need to slim down a bit before fledging.

Scientists think Manx shearwaters successfully find their way back home by using the sun as a compass, determining which direction to fly based on its position in the sky. But “to use the sun as a compass, you have to know what time of day it is,” lead author Patrick Lewin, an ecologist at the University of Oxford, tells NPR’s Geoff Brumfiel, since the sun’s overhead position changes throughout the day as the Earth rotates on its axis. Manx shearwaters rely on their internal clocks to help make sense of the sun’s movements and stay on track.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Scientists wondered whether the birds’ speedy east-bound homing journeys might be messing with their internal clocks—similar to jet lag in humans. They theorized that, as the birds zip across the ocean, their internal clocks do not keep pace with the changes to local time, which could affect their sun compasses and, in turn, their overall navigational accuracy.

To test this idea, researchers analyzed 20 years’ worth of GPS tracking data from 1,045 wild breeding Manx shearwaters. The birds made 3,688 trips between their breeding grounds and foraging grounds, but the scientists were most interested in their homing flights, so they isolated 1,837 of their eastward, home-bound journeys.

The researchers predicted that, as the birds headed east, jet lag would cause them to fly slightly off course in a clockwise direction. Those predictions were borne out by the data, which revealed that the birds veered clockwise by as much as 15 degrees.

To be sure jet lag was responsible for these small orientation errors, the team considered other possible factors, such as the strength of crosswinds and distance from the colony. But “the one thing that best predicted the observed changes in shearwaters’ orientation was always this sun compass effect,” Lewin tells NewScientist’s Michael Le Page.

The birds continued to fly slightly off course even when they were flying alongside coastlines, a surprising finding that suggests Manx shearwaters rely on multiple cues for navigation—and continue using multiple methods even when they give conflicting directions.

That makes sense to Sangeeta Rani, a chronobiologist at the University of Lucknow who was not involved with the research. “After all, if I have marked a path for myself in the woods, my innate ability is not to mindlessly follow the markings,” Rani tells Anirban Mukhopadhyay for ScienceNews. “It is to find out what’s missing and still find my way back.”

Rani adds that the birds’ reliance on multiple navigational methods could serve them well in the future, when climate change and human development could make the landscapes they’re familiar with unrecognizable.

Since Manx shearwaters are covering such long distances, these subtle detours probably don’t make that much of a difference to their overall journeys: The researchers calculated that, for a bird traveling roughly 620 miles, a seven-degree compass error would only add roughly three extra miles to the trip. This is probably why Manx shearwaters haven’t evolved some way of avoiding jet lag, the researchers posit.

The study focused only on Manx shearwaters, but the researchers suspect other creatures that travel long distances—more species of birds, as well as some bats and insects—might also experience jet lag. It probably doesn’t affect birds when they migrate, however, because most migrations follow north-south routes, Ken Cheng, an emeritus comparative cognition scholar at Macquarie University who was not involved with the study, tells NewScientist.
Now that scientists know Manx shearwaters experience jet lag, the next step is to understand whether and how it affects them.

“Do they mistime critical behaviors? Do they experience physiological side effects like we do?” Lewin says in a statement. “Perhaps these birds that routinely travel long distances could help teach us how to cope with and treat jet lag to avoid the really negative effects it can have on our health.”
