paras.en: From NASA and the Pentagon to start-ups, universities and international organizations, many entities depend on SpaceX’s Falcon 9. “Whenever you rely on one launch provider, especially one that’s commercial, you’re kind of at their whims,” says Kathleen Curlee, a senior research analyst at Georgetown University’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology.

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

The U.S. Department of Defense’s Space Force contracts using the Falcon 9 run through 2028, so those launches continue through that year, but Politico has reported that SpaceX has so far rebuffed Space Force efforts to secure further launches. Similarly, some companies have been unable to book future Falcon 9 flights as well, according to the Wall Street Journal. That means more uncertainties, and potential delays and cost increases for U.S. space launches.

Curlee expected such a decision by SpaceX. “I’m more surprised that people are so shocked this is happening,” she says. The company needs to pivot to its Starship program, she argues, and that may require retiring the Falcon family of rockets—not just the Falcon 9 but also the Falcon Heavy, a much beefier vehicle that also has partial reusability. Though Falcon 9 has been profitable, SpaceX’s business interests have been especially buoyed by Starlink, and the company is banking on the uncertain prospect of data centers in orbit, which would create yet more demand for Starship launches.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: In SpaceX’s early years, major launch contracts from NASA helped prop up the company, which at the time was struggling to attract customers while developing and deploying Falcon 9’s precursor, the Falcon 1. SpaceX ultimately became the biggest success story of NASA’s commercial crew and cargo programs, allowing the space agency to send astronauts to the International Space Station without relying on Russia’s Soyuz rocket. In this relationship, NASA now seems the one more in need of favors: the space agency books most of its orbital trips and deep-space launches through SpaceX but represents only a fraction of the company’s total launch business.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Joshua Finch, a NASA spokesperson, told Scientific American in a statement that “NASA and SpaceX are in regular communication and continue to work together on contract to launch cargo and crew for the safe operations of the International Space Station, as well as launch science, exploration, and research/technology missions through our launch services contracts.”

Finch also highlighted the agency’s collaboration with Boeing for astronauts’ trips to and from the space station. NASA had seen the company’s Starliner as a backup to SpaceX’s Crew Dragon, which flies atop the Falcon 9. Starliner has proven to be the much more expensive and less reliable option, however, with its development suffering numerous costly delays and its test flights going so poorly that one in 2024 stranded NASA astronauts at the space station for months. A Crew Dragon eventually brought that crew back home. NASA and Boeing plan for another uncrewed Starliner test flight as early as this December, followed by more crewed flights in 2028.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The Space Force has come to rely on SpaceX’s Falcon 9 (or its heftier cousin, the Falcon Heavy) for launches of sensitive national-security-related spacecraft, including those for the Golden Dome missile defense program. “I hope we don’t just lose this technology. It seems like a tremendous waste, if there isn’t some way for someone to pick up this program and keep it running,” says Matthew Weinzierl, a Harvard Business School researcher who studies the private space sector. He suggests it’s conceivable that the Space Force or other parts of the U.S. government could pay SpaceX to license the Falcon 9 technology, effectively taking control of the program and freeing the company to pursue other priorities. “There’s so much value. It seems strange to let it go,” he says.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: SpaceX did not respond to requests for comment. A Space Force spokesperson, Rose Riley, tells Scientific American that the agency has Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy launches planned through fiscal year 2032, and that as many as six other companies will soon be in a position to provide national security launch services as well. “We have an inherent duty to plan for possible contingencies,” Riley says. “While we don’t expect to have to use them, we are talking through all scenarios and what options we can leverage should we need to.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The prospects for Starship remain uncertain; its goal of full reusability would be a historic first for any orbital spacecraft—let alone the largest launch vehicle ever built. But many of its test flights so far have ended in fiery explosions; its next test, Flight 15, is slated for mid-November.

Even if SpaceX’s wildest dreams come true, with Starship soon entering routine service and ramping up to launch at an even higher cadence than Falcon 9, it’s unclear whether the huge rocket will have correspondingly huge demand. One glaring issue is that Starship presently lacks a payload fairing door of the sort most satellite customers currently need; instead it has a narrower aperture custom-made for ejecting batches of Starlink satellites. Another concern is the shifting landscape around artificial-intelligence-powering orbital data centers. On October 25 SpaceX continued its push into AI with a $40-billion debt-financing deal for data center GPUs, but the AI industry’s accumulation of debt now makes such deals more difficult. Despite that, Anthropic has reportedly become one of SpaceX’s biggest customers.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “Is this too big a risk? [SpaceX] takes big swings,” says Carissa Bryce Christensen, founder and CEO of BryceTech, an analytics and engineering contractor with NASA and the Space Force. Falcon 9 was once seen as unduly risky, too, she notes, when the rocket suffered high-visibility failures on its long path to routine flight and, eventually, industry dominance.

As SpaceX sunsets Falcon 9, some commercial customers are already scrambling to find new launch providers, Curlee says. The closest competitor to Starship, at least in the Earth-orbit launch market, is Blue Origin’s New Glenn, but that rocket exploded on its Cape Canaveral launchpad during a May 28 hotfire test and remains grounded. Blue Origin aims to have the pad and other infrastructure rebuilt by December. United Launch Alliance (ULA), a joint venture of Boeing and Lockheed Martin, has its new Vulcan Centaur rocket, which first flew in 2024 but is now grounded as well after problems with its solid rocket booster during a launch in February. ULA announced on October 28 that it’s resuming Vulcan spaceflights in mid-November.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Other competitors include Rocket Lab, which has mostly cornered the small-launch market, as well as rising companies such as Firefly Aerospace, Stoke Space and Relativity Space. “When there’s a big profit opportunity, there’s nothing more powerful for getting competition going than a lot of money sitting on the table, and this is probably one of those situations where there’s a lot of business to be had,” Weinzierl says.

Nevertheless, he points out, thanks to Falcon 9 helping to lower the bar for launch access in recent years, space start-ups have been able to scrape together money from investors to try new spacecraft designs. If that bar rises again and costs go up in the absence of SpaceX’s tried-and-true workhorse, those nascent companies might never get off the ground.

International competition has emerged on the horizon as well, especially from China’s expanding space sector, which is seeking to develop homegrown reusable rocketry to rival SpaceX. China has begun launching satellites for customers in countries such as Oman and Thailand over the past couple of years. But some potential customers may be hesitant to go that route because current U.S. law restricts contractors working with China or Chinese-owned companies. That means anyone that launches a spacecraft aboard a Chinese rocket may have trouble subsequently contracting with NASA or the Space Force.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Europe’s space industry remains behind the U.S. and China, though it is attempting to catch up. France’s Arianespace has a heavy-lift rocket called Ariane 6, and its partially reusable successor is in development for the 2030s. On October 5 European Space Agency chief Josef Aschbacher proposed investing €10 billion (about 11 billion USD) over the next decade to develop a new launch system to deliver astronauts to orbit. European governments will weigh the idea at a mid-December meeting in Rome.

“ESA’s priority is to ensure reliable, resilient and autonomous European access to space. Our baseline approach is therefore clear: for ESA missions, we look first to European launch services and seek to maximize their use,” said Kathryn Fleet, an ESA spokesperson, in a statement to Scientific American. Fleet points to the Ariane 6 rocket and Vega-C, a medium-lift rocket, while looking forward to emerging options. These include German start-up Isar Aerospace’s Spectrum rocket, which achieved its inaugural spaceflight in September, a milestone for the European commercial space sector. Fleet also said that working with Soyuz again is “not on the table,” because Soyuz launches from Europe’s spaceport in French Guiana were suspended in 2022 following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: SpaceX is, of course, led by CEO and almost-trillionaire Elon Musk, a mercurial figure active in far-right extremist politics in the U.S. and abroad. SpaceX has also swayed foreign policy, notably in Ukraine, such as by restricting Starlink Internet access.

So far, however, such incidents haven’t significantly affected SpaceX’s ability to ink lucrative government launch contracts, and federal agencies have found SpaceX to be the best option in terms of capability and price, Weinzierl says. He adds, “At the same time, no government wants to be reliant on a single company, so I imagine there will be substantial and sustained interest in supporting competitors to SpaceX.”

articles.title: Science advocates react to Democrats’ historic midterm rout: ‘It’s a new day in Washington’s

paras.en: Tuesday’s midterm election marked a sea change in the country’s political landscape, with Democrats sweeping control of Congress and making historic gains in many state legislatures. Now science advocates say they want answers for what has happened during the first two years of the Trump administration.

“It’s a new day in Washington,” says Gretchen Goldman, president and CEO of the Union of Concerned Scientists. “There’s huge opportunities for science, for democracy, for getting accountability for these attacks on science that we’ve seen. We are keen to get to work pushing back.”

Since taking office in 2025, the Trump administration has turned science into a battleground, slashing or outright canceling federal grants and research that was deemed too “woke.” Thousands of federal workers, including researchers, lost their jobs or decided to leave government. And the White House has pushed the country’s science funding to favor artificial intelligence and other technologies over other scientific fields, including medical research. At the same time, federal agencies have rolled back numerous anti-climate change measures in moves that critics say leave the country more vulnerable to warming and emissions.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The sweeping defeat exacted by Democrats on Tuesday is a stinging rebuke to those efforts, says Colette Delawalla, founder and CEO of advocacy group Stand Up for Science.
“Thinking through how all of this could pan out, this outcome is better than any eventuality that we that we worked through,” she says.

Democrats seized control of a majority of governorships for the first time since 2010, flipping races in Georgia, Iowa, Texas, Ohio and Nevada. Julie Scofield, a member of the coordinating committee for Defend Public Health, an advocacy organization, noted that Ohio’s new governor-elect is physician Amy Acton. She led Ohio’s public health system during the start of the COVID pandemic and was “very vocal about public health issues and concerns during her campaign,” Scofield says.

Among the winners in the Senate were several others with science backgrounds, including Abdul El-Sayed, who holds a medical degree and PhD in public health, in Michigan and pediatrician Annie Andrews in South Carolina.
Both candidates were supported by 314 Action, a political action committee that backs candidates with scientific expertise.
"Last night, scientists fought back and and won," says Shaughnessy Naughton, the organization's president. "This was a romp. The candidates worked hard and it's well deserved."

The victories also mean Democrats will take over key congressional committees and subcommittees, empowering them to help set the country’s science and health agenda. Russ Paulsen, president and CEO of Research!America, observes that, even under Republican leadership, Congress had acted as a check on the executive branch, restoring some of the cut grants and preventing some of the most controversial efforts to politicize science funding.

“We think that this bipartisan support is going to continue,” he says. “We hope that it will stay the priority that has been for these members and that they’ll begin to roll back the damage that the Office of Management [and] Budget (OMB) has done.”

One proposal from the OMB in particular, a set of rule changes that would have granted political appointees—and not area experts—control over which grants were approved, was voted down by Congress in a stopgap funding bill that passed in September. That bill expires in December, before the new Congress is sworn in. Paulsen says he is optimistic that the proposed rule changes will not be included in any bills passed during the lame duck session.

“The Congress that was sitting before this election will come and sit again,” he says. “They voted against this OMB overreach. There’s no reason to think that they won’t vote against the OMB overreach again.”

Delawalla speculates, however, that once the new Congress is sworn in, there will be a more aggressive tone toward certain Trump officials, such as Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., who has pushed to overhaul the country’s vaccine policies in ways that public health experts have said endanger Americans.

"His administration of HHS has been a unbelievable disaster, and I do look forward to Congress holding him accountable and making him answer for the disastrous decisions that he has made and inflicted on the American people, whether it's to our public health system, or mRNA research that has clearly shown unbelievable potential for better health outcomes," says Naughton.

At the same time, Democrats gaining power to set federal budget priorities presents opportunities to “restore some of the things that have really devastated the public health system over the last several years,” Scofield adds.
For example, President Donald Trump’s signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act, passed in 2025, includes massive cuts to Medicaid spending, a measure that Scofield says she hopes could be reversed.
“I think we have to understand that state and local public health departments rely heavily on federal funding. We have to restore that funding stream,” she says.

Improving funding to Medicare and Medicaid, as well as reestablishing subsidies and funding for the Affordable Care Act, must be "the number one issue" for Democrats in the near future, says Naughton.
Editor’s Note (11/4/26): This is a developing story and may be updated.

articles.title: The Super El Niño is already soaking the U.S. Expect more flooding to come

paras.en: A house floating down the San Juan River in Colorado, crumbling as it crashes into a bridge. A man evacuated from a palm tree surrounded by floodwaters in Brevard County, Florida. These are scenes from the “Super El Niño”–fueled rain events that are now soaking parts of the U.S.

This week the Southwest’s Four Corners region and Florida’s central coast have experienced major flood events, swamping homes and washing out roads. It was impossible to reach meteorologists in Pagosa Springs, Colorado, by phone on Tuesday because a major fiber cable in town had been cut by flooding, bringing down cell service.
Arleen Prochazka, a retired Air Force meteorologist who co-runs the nonprofit Pagosa Weather, managed to speak with Scientific American by email Wednesday.

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

“Homes were standing essentially in lakes,” she says. Back-to-back storms have made recovery difficult, she adds. “Most roads have deep potholes and are very rutted along the edges that flowed with water, mud and debris. Many roads are still impassable.”

And it’s not just the U.S.—in recent weeks Ecuador and Peru have experienced extreme soaking rains and floods, driven by the strong El Niño and what Daniel Swain, a climate scientist at the University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources, calls “absurd” ocean warming.
“We are seeing the hydroclimate effects of a very strong El Niño event occurring now but with a boost from climate change,” Swain says.

El Niño typically brings moisture-laden air to the desert Southwest in autumn. The climate pattern also boosts precipitation in Florida from fall to spring. In that sense, these events are precisely what would be expected, given the strength of the current El Niño.

Even so, the rainfall has been historic. In Malabar, Fla., two feet of rain fell in 36 hours over November 1 and November 2, according to the National Weather Service. It was a once-in-1,000-year event for the region, meaning that there is only a one-in-1,000 chance of such an extreme rainstorm in that area in a given year. One meteorologist estimated that 1.9 trillion gallons of water fell across Florida in 24 hours.

In the Four Corners region, which spans Colorado, New Mexico, Utah and Arizona, this week’s rainfall came on top of storms that, a little more than a week ago, dumped 100-year to 1,000-year levels of rainfall on parts of all four states. Flooding along the San Juan River during that event pushed the river’s crest to 15 feet. This week flows went even higher, with a river peak at 16.81 feet in the town of Pagosa Springs, Colo. The damage comes only a year after intense October 2025 flooding, driven by the remnants of Pacific cyclones.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “Getting essentially three of these big rainstorms in two years is very unusual,” says Russ Schumacher, a meteorologist at Colorado State University and Colorado’s state climatologist.

El Niño conditions provide a favorable jet stream for these autumn storms, Swain says, but this year’s event is supercharged by a marine heat wave off the West Coast of Central and North America. “Off the coast of Baja California, the water is 11 or 12 degrees Fahrenheit warmer than average,” he says. “That is astonishing.”
Ocean temperatures are also high in the Atlantic near Florida, he says, providing local storms with a “mind-boggling amount of moisture to work with.”

The NWS Climate Prediction Center forecasts a strong to very strong El Niño from January to March 2027. Florida will likely experience a winter of severe thunderstorms, Swain says, while the risk of flooding in the U.S. West will shift to California over the next few weeks.

articles.title: Newborn survival improves when families receive financial support
articles.author: Aimee Cunningham

paras.en: Extra financial support during pregnancy and after birth can help more babies thrive in their earliest days.

The Rx Kids program in Flint, Mich., launched in January 2024, provides extra cash to pregnant residents and their infants, unconditionally. Researchers compared neonatal deaths — those in the first four weeks of life — in 2025 with those in 2021 through 2024 in Flint. The city’s neonatal mortality rate dropped from 10 deaths per 1,000 live births to 5 deaths per 1,000 live births, researchers report November 2 in JAMA Pediatrics. The early neonatal mortality rate, covering deaths in the first week of life, fell from 8 per 1,000 to 2. For the rest of Michigan, rates were stable over the study’s time period.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “As a pediatrician, there is no outcome more important than babies surviving,” says Mona Hanna of the Michigan State University College of Human Medicine in Flint, who is also the founder and director of Rx Kids. “These early findings suggest that something as simple as providing families with financial support during pregnancy and infancy may help save babies’ lives.”

Income tends to drop and expenses rise in the months before and after a birth, making the perinatal period especially difficult financially for many families. Economic precarity can expose moms and babies to health harms. For example, housing instability and homelessness is associated with preterm birth and low birth weight.

Backed by public and private funds, Rx Kids got started in Flint, a city with a high rate of child poverty that has been dealing with the public health fallout of lead contamination in the water distribution system. Nearly 100 percent of the community participates in the program. Flint families receive $1,500 once during pregnancy and $500 per month in the baby’s first year. Anyone who is a resident, at least 16 weeks pregnant or with a newborn up to six months old can enroll. Families have put the extra cash toward diapers, transportation, housing and safe places for their babies to sleep, Hanna says.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “Every day, we hear from moms who tell us, ‘I can breathe’ or ‘A weight has been lifted off my shoulders.’ They tell us they feel less stressed, more hopeful, more supported and more loved,” Hanna says.

The support has had a measurable health impact, with studies linking the program to more access to prenatal care, a decrease in the preterm birth rate and in low-weight births and fewer neonatal intensive care admissions.
Rx Kids has now expanded to dozens of communities in Michigan and Ohio.

articles.title: Food contains thousands of overlooked chemicals. This physicist is mapping them
articles.author: Anna Mattson

paras.en: Computational physicist Giulia Menichetti is looking for “dark matter” in our food. In addition to known macronutrients, vitamins and minerals, the things we eat contain a whole world of natural chemicals we have no idea about. And those chemicals may affect our health.

“They have the ability to interact, to bind to human proteins, to modulate our microbiome,” says Menichetti of Harvard Medical School. “We want to leverage this to talk more and more about the role of food and nutrition in human health.”

Menichetti leads Foodome, a project to map our food’s full chemical complexity. Her team uses AI to mine scientific papers for every chemical compound that has ever been linked to a food. She singles out ones that haven’t been tracked by epidemiological studies — the “nutritional dark matter.” So far, her team has cataloged about 140,000 molecules.

When one hears about chemicals in food, they might initially think of artificial additives. Her team addresses those, but she’s also interested in naturally occurring chemicals. Take garlic, for example. Foodome has cataloged almost 7,000 different molecules in raw garlic alone. Some of these compounds have been investigated for health effects, but some are entirely new.

Foodome is still mining the scientific literature for these molecules and building out databases. Eventually, Menichetti would like AI to be able to predict how all these food molecules interact together and in the human body.

“There is a legacy of chemical complexity that comes from organisms that are all around us,” she says. “Food is part of that. It is actually our way to interact with our environment. We need to study it better.”

articles.title: Earwax’s surprisingly slippery but sticky properties deters insects
articles.author: Elizabeth Pennisi

paras.en: There are few things more annoying than having a bug fly into your ear. But the body is prepared to fend off these insect invasions, says David Hu, a bioengineer at Georgia Tech.

The goop inside our ears may act as a natural insect repellent, Hu’s team reports 28 October in Soft Matter. What we call earwax is not really waxy at all. Instead, the brownish substance absorbs water, a property that might help it regulate moisture in the ear and keep bugs out, the new analysis shows. “[This] familiar biological material may represent a sophisticated physical defense against small arthropods,” says Stanislav Gorb, a functional morphologist at the University of Kiel in Germany, who was not involved with the work.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Researchers have not studied earwax as much as other body fluids, such as snot, spit or even pee. “It’s a big mystery why we even have [it] in our ears,” Hu says. It can frankly seem like a nuisance. Earwax can build up, clogging earbuds and hearing aids and interfering with hearing, so understanding this substance better may help resolve those problems.

Hu and colleagues analyzed the mechanical and chemical properties of 36 earwax samples from pigs, sheep, dogs, cows, rabbits and humans. They also observed how fire ants (Solenopsis invicta) reacted to both natural and synthetic earwax.

Even though ants seem able to scale kitchen cabinets with ease to invade countertops, they flounder when they attempt to climb earwax. Hu thinks the earwax sucks moisture from the ants’ feet that helps them grip. But earwax also sticks to ants’ bodies, causing the insects to start grooming incessantly trying to get rid of it. “It’s both sticky and slippery,” Hu says.

The chemical analyses provide some clues about the origins of these properties. Dead skin cells make up 60 percent of earwax, along with a smattering of oils and moisture. The earwax contains pores that Hu believes may be shaped like ink bottles to help it absorb twice its weight in water and prevent water from sloshing around in the ear canal. Like snot, earwax has a huge range of consistencies.

Under normal conditions, earwax becomes dry and crumbly in about 10 weeks. As it dries, it’s moved outward by a layer of cells lining the ear canal that act as a cleaning conveyor belt. In this way, the ear maintains just the right thickness of earwax to keep insects at bay, Hu says. “It’s most potent when it’s thin,” he explains. “Too much, and the ants can use their tiny claws to grab hold and climb in.”

Hu admits there’s no practical way to turn earwax into a commercial insect repellent. Each person has a volume of earwax about equivalent to that of a grain of rice in each ear at any given time, says Hu, so even if you add up all the earwax on Earth, “it’s a pretty rare substance.” But, he adds, companies “are trying to come up with biodegradable and biofriendly ways to deal with insects.” And, says Gorb, perhaps earwax “could inspire a new generation of physical, nontoxic pest control surfaces,” that could provide coatings for protecting stored food, agricultural products and technology.

articles.title: The Human Brain May Organize Emotions Using a Hexagonal Grid
articles.author: Michelle Starr

paras.en: Nature may abhor a vacuum, but it adores a hexagonal grid.
The six-sided shape is an exquisitely efficient way of dividing space, from seafoam to honeycombs.
And now, scientists have found hints that the human brain uses this same geometry to organize our emotions.

Using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), a team of neuroscientists has detected a hexagonal signature in brain activity as people evaluate emotional information – suggesting that a grid-like system may help the brain sort this information.

"These findings suggest that emotion knowledge is structured by a grid-like coordinate system in the human brain," write neuroscientists Yumeng Ma and Philip A. Kragel of Emory University in a paper published in PLOS Biology.
We often consider emotions one of the messier parts of being human. They can be fleeting or enduring, contradictory, overwhelming, and difficult to understand, even for the person experiencing them.
Yet how we feel about the world seems to be vitally important. Emotions help us assess risks, make decisions, respond to changing circumstances, and form bonds with others.
When our ability to experience or regulate emotions is disrupted, the effects can ripple through almost every aspect of our lives.
So, in order to navigate the world, we need to be able to recognize emotions, distinguish between them, and understand how they relate to one another.
And although scientists have long known that our understanding of emotions follows a surprisingly orderly structure, exactly how the brain codifies that structure has remained a mystery.
For decades, researchers have described emotions along two axes. There's valence, which refers to how pleasant or unpleasant an emotion is; and arousal, which is how calming or activating it is.

Together, they make up the affective circumplex, a two-dimensional map of emotional concepts. Contentment and excitement, for example, may both be pleasant, but one is calming and the other considerably less so. Likewise, anger and elation are similarly highly activating, but are at opposite ends of the valence axis.
There are, however, clues from other studies investigating how the brain organizes and represents information – such as spatial information about our surroundings.
And this brings us to a type of neuron known as the grid cell.
First identified in rats in 2005, grid cells are neurons that become active when an animal moves through particular locations in its environment.

But here's the really fascinating detail. If you plot all the places where a particular grid cell lights up on a map of the animal's surroundings, they form a repeating pattern of equilateral triangles, creating a grid with sixfold, or hexagonal, symmetry.
That is, a single cell lights up when the rat visits the center or any of the six corners of an imaginary hexagon – and the pattern repeats across the animal's surroundings.
Different grid cells respond to different arrangements of locations, collectively giving the brain a coordinate system that helps the animal track where it is as it moves.

But grid-like coding may not be limited to navigating physical spaces. Previous research has found evidence that the brain uses similar patterns of neuronal activity to organize abstract information, from visual concepts to the relative value of different choices.
And that raised an intriguing possibility. If emotions can be organized on a two-dimensional map, could the brain use the same kind of coordinate system to navigate them?

Ma and Kragel studied 18 people and showed them "emotion-laden stimuli" – facial expressions morphing from one emotion to another, and sequences of emotionally evocative phrases – while taking non-invasive fMRI images of their brain activity.

Each stimulus involved a transition across the affective circumplex, which allowed the researchers to track brain activity as the participants followed movement through this two-dimensional emotional 'space'.
In a region of the brain called the ventromedial prefrontal cortex, the researchers detected the telltale signature of a hexagonal grid as the study participants thought about emotional states.

Brain activity varied according to the direction of movement through the emotional map, following a repeating pattern of sixfold symmetry – just as grid-like coding does when the brain navigates physical space.

What's more, the pattern appeared regardless of whether participants were evaluating facial expressions or written phrases, suggesting that the brain was encoding the relationships between emotional concepts, rather than just reacting to what the participants saw.

The researchers also found that brain activity reflected the distance between emotional concepts on the affective circumplex – and that this signal was associated with how participants judged changes in emotional information.

Now, there are some limitations. The study was pretty small – 18 people is not a large cohort – and further research will be needed to understand how this grid-like system operates and whether it plays a direct role in how we process emotional information.
Still, it's a very intriguing result – suggesting that the brain may use the same principles to organize our emotional world as it does to navigate the physical one.

"These findings," the researchers write, "suggest that the structure evident in self-report may reflect how the brain organizes emotion knowledge using mechanisms similar to those implicated in spatial and conceptual navigation."
The research has been published in PLOS Biology.

articles.title: People Started to Take Cold Showers in an Experiment, And a Strange Thing Happened
articles.author: Peter Dockrill

paras.en: If you're not used to cold showers, they're not exactly for the faint of heart.
Opting to immerse your naked body in a torrent of frigid water might even seem like pure masochism, but evidence suggests there are reasons to take the plunge.

In a series of experiments, psychologist Lena Glaser investigated the effects of people having cold showers, as part of a broader study into the psychological factors involved when people are urged to adopt new behaviors.
The research, completed as part of Glaser's doctoral dissertation at the University of Basel in Switzerland, uncovered a striking finding.

In a pooled analysis of three randomized controlled trials involving 719 people, participants who regularly took cold showers reported 31 percent fewer days off work due to illness, compared with those who didn't regularly take cold showers.
The cold shower group also saw a 26 percent reduction in reported illness days, compared to the participants who mostly took warm showers.

In addition, participants taking cold showers reported slightly improved psychological well-being in questionnaires during the experiment. They also reported signs of improved physical well-being, but the measurement was not statistically significant.

According to Glaser, many participants dropped out in the first two weeks of the experiment, but the dropout rate declined after that. Among those who stuck with it at least 70 percent of the time, an average of 77.3 to 90 percent reported taking cold showers in any given week, depending on the trial.
"That suggests people gradually get used to it," Glaser says.

The key findings echo a 2016 study, which similarly found that people taking cold showers showed a 29 percent reduction in absence from work due to illness, although it didn't observe a reduction in days when people felt ill.

"Our pooled analysis shows a clear reduction in both illness days and sickness absence, suggesting a robust effect that translates directly into improved work attendance and reduced productivity loss," Glaser and fellow researchers write in their preprint paper, which has been submitted to the Journal of Health Psychology.
With regard to the well-being effects, the researchers suggest the benefits of cold showers extend beyond illness prevention and can deliver a more holistic improvement in people's well-being.

"Crucially, the observed improvement in well-being directly refutes the common initial concern that a cold shower intervention would lead to a worsening of the participants' well-being or comfort," the team writes.

"Our findings on improved well-being suggest that cold showers might offer [an] effective method for improving mental and physical health, thereby potentially reducing the risk factors that lead to sickness absence in the first place."

It's worth noting that the findings have not yet been peer-reviewed, the results come from self-reported data provided by the participants during the experiment, and participants were grouped by how often they actually took cold showers rather than at random.

But if future studies can confirm and replicate these results, cold showers could make for a simple, low-cost intervention in workplaces that promotes employees' health while curbing absenteeism, the researchers say.
As to what it is about cold showers that might provide benefits to health, this study didn't look at the biological mechanisms.

But a study published in 2024 found that people who took cold showers showed increased signals of immune response, suggesting that repeated exposure to cold water might confer benefits to immunity, and similar effects have been seen in studies investigating cold water immersion.
If so, it's possible those immune effects could translate into fewer days when people fall ill – and fewer days missing work as a result – but we'll need more research to confirm the theory.
For now, if you want to try taking cold showers yourself, Glaser suggests starting off slowly, gradually dropping the temperature over time, and experimenting with it to stay comfortable.
"The water doesn't have to be equally cold every day," she says.
"It's important to listen to your body and pay attention to how you feel. But sometimes it's worth pushing yourself a little."
The findings are reported in Lena Glaser's doctoral dissertation, available on the University of Basel's website.

articles.title: Ancient DNA Rewrites The Story of How Germanic And Celtic Languages Spread Across Europe
articles.author: Jess Cockerill

paras.en: Hundreds of millions of people today speak Germanic languages: English, Dutch, German, Danish, Swedish, etc.
Archaeologists and linguists have many unanswered questions when it comes to the origins of these languages, as well as the mostly endangered Celtic languages that were once widespread.

"DNA sequences do not tell us directly which language people spoke. But by combining ancient DNA with linguistic and archaeological evidence, we can begin to trace how languages spread and changed over thousands of years," explains geneticist Eske Willerslev, a geneticist at the University of Copenhagen.
In two complementary papers, Willerslev and team trace the spread of Germanic and Celtic languages across ancient Europe.
Both papers are published today in Nature, here and here.
First, the researchers sequenced 712 new genomes from ancient (mostly Iron Age) humans across Europe, and analyzed these alongside 4,009 others.
Then, they used the data to reconstruct how genetic groups migrated, comparing these movements to cultural evidence like runic inscriptions, pottery, and styles of burial and architecture.
The researchers were surprised to find that people had migrated from somewhere around the Baltic region – likely between Finland and northeastern Sweden – into Denmark and Sweden's south.
"This population… offers a potential vector for the introduction of the Germanic language group to Scandinavia, some 800 years later than traditionally assumed," the team writes.
Within about 500 years, the genes of these newcomers were well and truly mixed into the human population throughout Scandinavia.

"For over a century, scholars have debated when and from where the Germanic languages arrived in Northern Europe. What is exciting is that we can now test some of these ideas directly," says the paper's lead author, geneticist Hugh McColl.
"We discovered a previously unknown migration that occurred at exactly the time and place where we would expect the earliest form of Germanic to be spreading."

Then, around 1,650 years ago, people from southern Scandinavia began moving down into the countries we now know as Germany, Poland, and the Netherlands, where, at the time, people were probably speaking Celtic languages.

"Archaeologists and linguists had not predicted it, but it helps explain several cultural and linguistic connections between Scandinavia and Britain that have puzzled researchers for a long time," McColl says.
People were also migrating back towards Scandinavia, at about the same time Old Norse emerged.
Meanwhile, leading theories say that Celtic languages originated on Europe's Atlantic coast, but the new ancient DNA evidence challenges that.

During the Iron Age (about 2,500 years ago), Celtic languages were spoken across the continent of Europe. Today, just a few of these languages survive, in pockets of the northwestern Atlantic coast. There are the Goidelic languages: Irish, Manx, and Scottish Gaelic; and the Brittonic languages: Welsh, Cornish, and Breton.
For this study, the researchers used the same set of data as they did for the Germanic study, but left out some of the newer genomes and added a few from locations more relevant to Celtic history.

The new evidence suggests Celtic languages were spread during a westward migration of people around 3,000 years ago, from the Urnfield culture in eastern central Europe into France, Britain, Ireland, the Iberian Peninsula, and Italy.
"The question of where Celtic languages came from has been debated for more than 100 years," says comparative linguist Guus Kroonen.
"Ancient DNA gives us an entirely new way to evaluate competing theories and brings important new evidence into the discussion."

articles.title: Permanent daylight saving time has a dark side, scientists warn

paras.en: Permanent daylight saving time has a dark side, scientists warn

- A new study warns that permanent daylight saving time could force American children to make at least 2 billion additional school commutes in darkness, potentially increasing safety risks and disrupting their biological clocks. Researchers found that fatal crashes involving school-aged pedestrians were roughly twice as likely during dark mornings as after sunrise.

Keeping daylight saving time in effect all year could bring brighter evenings, but new research suggests the change would come with a troubling consequence for American children. A nationwide switch could result in at least 2 billion additional trips to school in darkness, potentially increasing safety risks while reducing children's exposure to important morning sunlight.

The debate over permanent daylight saving time has gained momentum in Washington, D.C. This past summer, the U.S. House of Representatives approved legislation that would eliminate the annual return to standard time in the fall. Nineteen states, including Washington, have already approved measures supporting the change, which would take effect in those states if the federal bill becomes law.

The legislation remains stalled in the Senate, with school start times emerging as a major concern. Permanent daylight saving time (DST) would push sunrise an hour later during the winter months, leaving mornings darker from November through March. Although this would affect everyone traveling early in the day, researchers at the University of Washington wanted to understand what it would mean specifically for children heading to school.
Permanent Daylight Saving Time Could Add Billions of Dark School Commutes

To measure the potential impact, the research team examined 14 of the 19 states that have already approved permanent daylight saving time measures. They combined school enrollment figures, individual school start times, and geographic coordinates to determine how frequently students would need to travel to school before sunrise. The researchers then calculated the total number of these trips under the proposed system and compared it with the current practice of changing clocks twice a year.

The results revealed substantial increases. In Washington state alone, permanent daylight saving time would produce nearly 35 million additional school commutes in darkness. Similar patterns emerged across the other 13 states, with Georgia showing the largest increase at approximately 71 million additional dark trips.

When the researchers extended their findings to estimate the nationwide impact, they calculated that permanent daylight saving time would create at least 2 billion more trips to school before sunrise compared with the current system.

The potential consequences go beyond inconvenient mornings. An analysis of U.S. traffic collision records found that fatal crashes involving school-aged pedestrians were roughly twice as likely to occur during dark mornings as after sunrise. The findings were published October 29 in the journal Current Biology.

"It's called the 'Sunshine Protection Act' because you get an extra hour of light at the end of the day. But you will take that hour from the morning. You could call it the Sunshine Destruction Act," said senior author Horacio de la Iglesia, a professor of biology at the University of Washington. "These dark mornings will inequitably affect children who have to go to school at a certain time. It's a very tangible metric that anybody from any state or socioeconomic background can relate to. Nobody wants their kids to go to school in the dark."

paras.en: Why Morning Sunlight Matters for Children's Health

Beyond concerns about traffic safety, losing access to morning sunlight could interfere with the body's natural daily rhythms. Bright light early in the day helps synchronize the circadian clock, the internal timing system that influences sleep, mood, appetite, and other important functions. When people receive too little morning light, maintaining these biological rhythms can become more difficult.
For children, who must typically follow fixed school schedules, darker mornings could mean missing a valuable opportunity to receive daylight at a time when their bodies need it.

"When we send kids to school in the dark, we are depriving them from an opportunity to get that morning daylight," said lead author Guadalupe Rodríguez Ferrante, a postdoctoral researcher in biology at the University of Washington. "We were asking what's the cost for these children. We wanted actual numbers, a real number of kids based on the geographic location of each school."

The researchers also identified which communities would experience the greatest changes. Schools located near the western boundaries of time zones, including those in Forks, Washington, would be particularly affected because sunrise already occurs relatively late in those locations. Districts that begin classes early in the morning would face similarly large increases in dark commutes.

Mississippi and Alabama offer striking examples. Schools in both states begin, on average, before 8 a.m. Under the current clock system, each state has approximately 2 million school trips in darkness. With permanent daylight saving time, that figure would rise to more than 20 million trips per state.

"Some districts probably never experience a dark commute under the current system, and, if this passes, suddenly they will wake up to this new reality that their kids are going to school in the dark," Rodríguez Ferrante said. "Keep in mind that we used the actual start time listed for each school, and a lot of schools offer breakfast or other things before school, so the kids could be getting there even earlier."
Why the 2 Billion Estimate May Be Too Low

Although the researchers used detailed school information to calculate changes in 14 states, their nationwide estimate required broader assumptions. To project what would happen if the entire United States adopted permanent daylight saving time, they assumed students would generally be leaving for school at around 8 a.m.
Because many children begin traveling earlier, the team believes the projected increase of approximately 2 billion dark commutes may substantially underestimate the actual impact.
"For the estimation, we assumed students would be leaving home around 8 a.m.," Rodríguez Ferrante said. "That's pretty late, so our calculation is likely an underestimation of the real number."

The findings also raise questions about efforts to improve teenagers' sleep by delaying high school start times. Adolescents typically have biological clocks that shift later than those of younger children and adults, making later school schedules beneficial. The researchers argue that permanently moving clocks forward could undermine some of those gains by making morning sunlight less accessible.

One possible solution would be to start school later to compensate for the darker mornings. However, de la Iglesia argues that such a change could have ripple effects throughout daily life, potentially requiring families and workplaces to adjust their schedules as well.

"I've heard the argument, 'If we're in permanent DST, we can just delay the school start time to address these issues,'" de la Iglesia said. "Well, if we do that, you will end up going to work later. And everything is going to get delayed. You will get out of work an hour later, and you will miss the opportunity to enjoy your evening light. And essentially, we're just going to be realigning everybody to solar time. That, by definition, is Standard Time."

The researchers' findings highlight a central tradeoff in the debate over permanent daylight saving time. While eliminating seasonal clock changes would provide more evening sunlight during winter, the additional daylight would come at the expense of morning light, potentially affecting children's safety, sleep, and daily routines.

Additional study authors include high school student Daniel Zhang and University of Washington biology undergraduates Nirekh Dasika, Alicia Nam, Jessie Lu, Navneet Tumber, Elena Kully-Rivera, Viridian Klei, and Micaela E. Romero.

Over a billion more dark-morning school commutes for Kâ12 children under the Sunshine Protection Act. Current Biology, 2026; DOI: 10.1016/j.cub.2026.10.014

articles.title: Scientists may have finally explained why our brains and bodies are cross-wired

paras.en: Scientists may have finally explained why our brains and bodies are cross-wired

- Scientists propose that the brainâs mysterious cross-wiring, which connects each hemisphere to the opposite side of the body, may have originated more than 500 million years ago in the visual systems of ancient fish. Rather than evolving for a specific advantage, this unusual arrangement may simply be a legacy of evolution building new brain circuits on an ancient foundation.

Why does the left side of the brain control the right side of the body, while the right side controls the left? This unusual arrangement is one of the most intriguing features of the nervous system, and scientists have proposed a new explanation that reaches back hundreds of millions of years.

Dr. Martin Wessendorf, a neuroscientist and associate professor emeritus at the University of Minnesota, studies how the brainstem regulates neurons in the spinal cord. Daniel Wang specializes in cognitive neuroscience and neurodegenerative diseases. Together, they have examined the evolutionary origins of the brain's crossed connections.

In a study published in Frontiers in Neuroanatomy, the researchers explore several neural circuits in four-limbed animals that are cross-wired (meaning one side of the brain connects with the opposite side of the body). Their hypothesis suggests that these connections may have developed because evolution built new brain circuits around an ancient visual system.

The brain contains numerous pathways that cross from one side of the central nervous system to the other. Understanding why these contralateral (midline-crossing) connections exist requires examining how different sensory and movement circuits developed over evolutionary time.
How the Brain Processes Visual Information

One possible explanation begins with the eyes. When light passes through the eye's lens, the image projected onto the retina is reversed. Objects appearing to our right are projected onto the left side of the retina, while objects on our left are projected onto the right.

Visual information travels along the optic nerve to a structure called the optic chiasm. Here, nerve fibers are organized so that information from the right visual field reaches the left side of the brain, while information from the left visual field is directed to the right side.

Some of these signals reach an ancient brain structure called the optic tectum (which in mammals is called the superior colliculus). Located in the midbrain, this region helps produce fast reactions to visual events, such as suddenly noticing something moving nearby.

Each side of the optic tectum contains a representation of the opposite visual field. Deeper within the structure, information about physical sensations (somatosensory information) is also organized into corresponding maps.

Because the optic tectum exists in every vertebrate species, it is considered one of the most ancient structures in the vertebrate nervous system. Its early appearance may be especially important for understanding why so many other neural pathways cross sides.
Why Sensory Signals Cross the Brain and Spinal Cord

The researchers also examined two major pathways responsible for transmitting sensations from the body to the brain. Both cross the center of the central nervous system (the brain and spinal cord), and both appear to be widespread among tetrapods (the animals with four limbs, including mammals, birds, reptiles, and amphibians).

The first, called the dorsal column pathway, carries information about gentle touch, vibration, and the position of different body parts. Signals from the limbs and torso travel upward through the dorsal portion of the spinal cord before reaching another neuron in the brainstem, just above the spinal cord. From there, the pathway crosses to the opposite side.

Although fish lack this pathway, scientists have identified it in amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals. Its presence across these major animal groups suggests that the arrangement emerged early in tetrapod evolution and has remained largely conserved.

The second pathway, known as the spinothalamic tract, transmits sensations involving pain, itching, and certain types of touch. Unlike the dorsal column pathway, it crosses to the opposite side within the spinal cord itself.
After crossing, signals travel upward to the thalamus, a brain region located above the midbrain that plays a central role in processing sensory and movement information.

This crossed arrangement is found in birds, mammals, and reptiles. It also occurs in some cartilaginous fish, including sharks and rays, suggesting that aspects of this organization have even deeper evolutionary roots.
How the Brain Controls Movement Across the Body

The crossed organization of the nervous system extends beyond sensation. The researchers identified three important pathways involved in controlling skeletal muscles that also connect one side of the brain with the opposite side of the spinal cord.
The first is the tectospinal pathway, which helps the body respond rapidly to information from the environment.

The optic tectum processes more than vision. It also receives information about sounds and physical sensations, organizing these signals into maps that align with its visual representation on the opposite side of the brain.

Imagine preparing to cross a street when you suddenly notice a car approaching from the corner of your eye. You instinctively turn toward the vehicle. The tectospinal pathway is one of the neural circuits that helps produce this rapid response. It can also coordinate similar reactions to unexpected sounds or touch.

The movement signals originate in the deepest layers of the optic tectum and travel through nerve fibers to the opposite side of the spinal cord. This pathway is present in most tetrapods and certain cartilaginous fish.

Another important circuit is the rubrospinal pathway, which is thought to help animals control their limbs. It begins in a midbrain structure called the red nucleus and extends to the opposite side of the spinal cord. The pathway is especially prominent in most mammals, although it has also been identified in other tetrapods and some cartilaginous fish.
The Evolution of Fine Motor Control in Humans
The third pathway, called the corticospinal tract, has a particularly important role in humans because it supports precise movements, including the fine control of our fingers.
Its evolutionary history is more complicated than that of the other pathways.

All vertebrates possess a telencephalon, the forward portion of the brain that accounts for much of the brain's overall size in humans. However, only mammals have a cerebral cortex organized into six distinct layers.
This six-layered cortex supports sophisticated functions such as combining sensory information with memories, coordinating movement, and processing language.
The corticospinal pathway extends from the cerebral cortex toward the spinal cord, but its function varies among animals.
In most mammals, it primarily influences sensory processing. Nerve fibers reach spinal cord regions that receive information from the body, allowing the brain to regulate incoming sensations.

In primates (including humans) and certain other animals capable of highly precise movements, the pathway also reaches spinal cord regions responsible for controlling muscles. These connections make intricate actions possible, including the coordinated finger movements needed for delicate tasks.
Depending on the species, the corticospinal tract can regulate sensory information or contribute directly to movement. In either case, its fibers cross the midline of the nervous system.

The researchers suggest that humans may have developed advanced fine motor abilities by adapting an older neural circuit originally involved in controlling sensory input. Rather than creating an entirely new system, evolution may have given an existing pathway an additional purpose.
A 500-Million-Year-Old Explanation for the Brain's Crossed Wiring
Taken together, these neural pathways point toward a potentially surprising explanation for the brain's unusual organization.

The researchers propose that the earliest visual circuits helped establish a pattern in which sensory and movement pathways were organized across opposite sides of the nervous system. Later circuits may have inherited this arrangement as they evolved, particularly in tetrapods.

Because every living vertebrate possesses an optic chiasm and an optic tectum organized around information from the opposite visual field, the researchers suspect that these structures were already present in primitive jawless fish during the Cambrian Period, approximately 538 to 486 million years ago.
If correct, this would mean that the basic organization underlying the brain's crossed connections began developing more than half a billion years before modern humans appeared.

The hypothesis may even be testable. Scientists could examine fossilized skulls from ancient jawless fish for anatomical evidence that might help establish whether these early animals possessed an optic chiasm and optic tectum.
An Evolutionary Inheritance Rather Than an Advantage?
The broader idea challenges the assumption that every unusual biological feature must have evolved because it provided a direct survival benefit.

Evolution often modifies structures that already exist instead of developing completely new systems. Once the ancient visual pathways established a crossed organization, that arrangement may have influenced how additional sensory and motor circuits developed.
In particular, the organization of the visual system (and in particular, the optic tectum) may have provided a structural foundation that later pathways followed.

Under this hypothesis, the brain's crossed connections did not necessarily arise because controlling the opposite side of the body was inherently more effective. Instead, they may reflect the lasting influence of an ancient arrangement that evolution repeatedly reused.

The result could be one of the most enduring examples of how the nervous system preserves its evolutionary history. The strange relationship between the brain's two hemispheres and the opposite sides of the body may ultimately trace back to the visual systems of animals that lived more than 500 million years ago.

- Martin W. Wessendorf, Daniel Delie Wang. Why is the right side of the brain responsible for the left side of the body? The evolutionary history of a puzzling trait. Frontiers in Neuroanatomy, 2026; 20 DOI: 10.3389/fnana.2026.1937941

articles.title: A surprising discovery could help aging muscles repair themselves

paras.en: A surprising discovery could help aging muscles repair themselves

- Scientists have discovered a compound that transforms a natural muscle-repair protein into a more powerful version dubbed "Super HGF," more than doubling its ability to bind to a key receptor while protecting it from age-related chemical damage. The breakthrough, supported by early mouse experiments, could eventually help combat muscle loss and preserve strength as people age.

Muscles can begin losing their strength and ability to recover surprisingly early in the aging process. Over time, muscle tissue may develop scar tissue, accumulate fat, and lose some of the specialized fibers responsible for rapid, powerful movements. These changes can make everyday activities more difficult and gradually reduce mobility and physical independence.

Now, scientists in Japan have identified a promising molecule that could help protect the body's natural muscle repair system and potentially make it more effective. In laboratory experiments, the compound strengthened an important biological signal involved in muscle regeneration, increasing its ability to connect with a key cellular receptor by more than twofold.

The discovery comes from a team led by Professor Ryuichi Tatsumi at Kyushu University's Faculty of Agriculture. Their findings, published in Scientific Reports, suggest a possible new approach to addressing the cellular changes that make aging muscles increasingly difficult to repair.
How Aging Disrupts the Body's Muscle Repair System

Skeletal muscles are the muscles attached to bones that allow us to walk, lift objects, maintain posture, and perform other voluntary movements. Although these muscles experience wear and tear throughout life, they also have a remarkable ability to repair themselves.

Much of that repair depends on specialized stem cells known as satellite cells. These cells normally remain inactive, positioned alongside muscle fibers until they receive a signal that repair or regeneration is needed. Once activated, they can multiply and develop into muscle cells that help restore damaged tissue.

An essential part of this process involves a protein called hepatocyte growth factor, or HGF. Despite its name, HGF plays important roles beyond the liver, including helping activate the stem cells responsible for muscle regeneration.

Under normal conditions, HGF is stored within the supportive material surrounding muscle fibers. When muscles experience an injury or mechanical stimulation, such as physical movement or stretching, the protein can be released.

HGF then attaches to a receptor called c-met on the surface of satellite cells. Receptors are specialized proteins that receive molecular signals and trigger responses inside cells. In this case, the interaction helps awaken dormant satellite cells, allowing them to multiply, mature, and participate in repairing muscle fibers.
But this carefully coordinated system becomes less reliable with age.
A Hidden Chemical Change May Weaken Aging Muscles

The researchers' previous work revealed that HGF can undergo a chemical modification known as nitration. This process attaches a chemical group called a nitro group to particular locations on a protein, potentially changing its structure and interfering with its normal activity.
For HGF, the researchers identified two especially important locations, Y198 and Y250. Both lie within the region involved in attaching to the c-met receptor.
When these sites undergo nitration, HGF becomes less capable of connecting with its receptor. The result is similar to a key that has become damaged and can no longer operate its intended lock.

This disruption could have important consequences for aging muscles. Even if the body continues producing HGF, chemical changes may prevent the protein from properly activating the stem cells needed for tissue repair. The researchers believe this mechanism may contribute to age-related muscle wasting and declining regenerative capacity.

"HGF is not necessarily missing as we age," explains Tatsumi. "Rather, it can be chemically altered after it is made. That led us to wonder whether a compound with strong antioxidant capacity might protect HGF, either by preventing nitration or by compensating for the functional loss it causes."
Scientists Test Two Powerful Sulfur Compounds
To investigate that possibility, the team studied two compounds with strong antioxidant properties: glutathione trisulfide (GSSSG) and lipoic acid trisulfide (LASSS).

Antioxidants can help limit certain types of chemical damage caused by reactive molecules. Such damage can interfere with proteins and other essential components of cells, particularly when the body's normal protective systems become less effective.

The two compounds belong to a chemical family called trisulfides. Their defining feature is a chain of three sulfur atoms connected to one another. This arrangement gives them unusual chemical properties, including an ability to participate in reactions involving the transfer of electrons, known as redox reactions.
Because these reactions play important roles in cellular chemistry, trisulfides have attracted growing interest as potential ingredients in new medicines.

In the first set of experiments, both compounds reduced nitration at the two vulnerable sites on HGF. However, preventing this chemical modification did not completely restore the protein's ability to attach to c-met.
The scientists therefore increased the amount of trisulfide used relative to HGF. They changed the molar ratio, which compares the number of molecules of each substance, from 1:4000 to 1:8000.
That adjustment produced an unexpected result.
An Unexpected Discovery Creates "Super HGF"
At the higher concentration, LASSS did much more than protect HGF from chemical damage. It also dramatically improved the protein's ability to bind to its receptor.

Compared with untreated HGF, the protein exposed to LASSS showed more than twice the binding affinity for c-met. In other words, it could attach to its target receptor much more strongly, potentially enhancing a critical step in the muscle repair process.
The treatment also made HGF more resistant to the loss of function caused by nitration, particularly at the Y198 site.
Notably, the effect was specific to LASSS. Although GSSSG had also reduced nitration in the earlier experiments, it did not produce the same improvement in receptor binding.

"This exceeded our expectations," comments Tatsumi. "We knew trisulfides had diverse biological functions, but we never expected that simply mixing HGF with LASSS would produce such a striking effect.

"What this tells us is that LASSS does more than simply neutralize reactive molecules. It may interact directly with HGF and induce a subtle structural change, creating an enhanced 'Super HGF' form that binds c-met more strongly and resists nitration."

The researchers suspect that LASSS interacts with HGF in a way that slightly alters the protein's three-dimensional shape. Because a protein's shape helps determine how well it interacts with other molecules, even a small structural adjustment could substantially change its activity.
The result is what the team describes as "Super HGF," a potentially enhanced form of the body's existing muscle repair signal.

Importantly, stronger receptor binding does not automatically establish that muscle regeneration itself has improved. Additional experiments will be needed to determine whether this molecular enhancement translates into better muscle healing and strength.
Mouse Experiments Reveal Promising Protection
After observing the effects in laboratory experiments, the researchers wanted to determine whether LASSS could also protect HGF inside living muscle tissue.

They used mice subjected to tail suspension, an established experimental method for studying muscle atrophy. By reducing normal weight bearing and muscle use, this technique produces some of the changes associated with prolonged inactivity, including muscle deterioration.

Mice that received LASSS before the experiment showed significantly less HGF nitration than untreated animals. This suggested that the compound's ability to protect the muscle repair protein was not limited to controlled laboratory conditions.
Once again, GSSSG failed to produce the same protective result.

These findings provide early evidence that LASSS can influence the chemical processes affecting HGF within living animals. However, the mouse experiments demonstrated protection against nitration, not that LASSS restored lost muscle mass or improved physical strength.
The researchers emphasize that studies involving aging animals are still necessary to establish the compound's effectiveness and safety in vivo, meaning within a living organism.
A Potential New Strategy Against Age-Related Muscle Loss
The discovery could eventually contribute to treatments aimed at maintaining muscle function during aging or extended periods of inactivity.

Muscle deterioration is not limited to older adults. It can also occur during prolonged bed rest or other situations in which muscles are used less frequently. When muscle repair mechanisms become impaired, recovering lost strength and function can become especially challenging.

Rather than replacing the body's natural repair machinery, the approach explored in this study seeks to protect and enhance an existing biological signal. If the benefits can be confirmed in future studies, strengthening HGF activity could become one strategy for supporting muscle regeneration.

The scientists also believe that the underlying effects of LASSS on HGF may extend across species. That raises the possibility of applications not only in human medicine but also in veterinary care, particularly for aging companion animals such as dogs and cats.

For now, the findings represent an early step toward understanding how a naturally occurring muscle repair pathway might be strengthened. Whether LASSS can safely and effectively preserve muscle function during aging remains an open question.

Still, the unexpected discovery that a sulfur-based compound can both protect and enhance a critical repair protein offers a promising direction for future research, with the long-term goal of helping people maintain mobility, independence, and a better quality of life as they grow older.

articles.title: Mars isn't dead — recent volcanic activity reveals it's just sleeping
articles.author: Robert Lea

paras.en: Scientists have long suspected that Mars is geologically "dead," but new spacecraft observations suggest the Red Planet's volcanoes are merely sleeping.

That means that Olympus Mons, the extinct Martian volcano that at around 16 miles (26 kilometers) above the surrounding Martian plains is the largest mountain in the solar system, may in fact be a slumbering giant.

The observations were made with the European Space Agency (ESA) mission ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) as it studied volcanic fissures along the Alba Mons region of the Red Planet. Alba Mons is in the Tharsis region of Mars, the same area that is home to Olympus Mons. While the latter is the tallest volcano in the solar system, at 374 miles (600 km) across, about the size of Arizona, the Alba Mons region is the largest volcano when considering surface area.

TGO detected gas containing hydrogen chloride making its way to the surface of Mars through the Alba Mons fissures. The same gas is commonly found escaping from magmatic vents on Earth, with the compound coming from hot magma beneath the surface. Detecting it on Mars is a sign of dormant Martian volcanism.

Orbital imagery had previously shown some volcanoes appear to have been active within the last few million years, and seismometers have detected the rumbling of "marsquakes," both implying the Red Planet is volcanically active. However, eruptions and lava flows have been conspicuous by their absence.

"Our findings suggest that Mars has retained enough internal heat to support volcanic activity until recently, and possibly still does," team co-leader and scientist at the Space Research Centre of the Polish Academy of Sciences, Daniel Mège, said in a statement sent to Space.com via email. "The TGO was able to find the smoking gun. It was like looking for a needle in a haystack."
Evidence of dormant Martian volcanism is rising

Mège and colleagues were first alerted to something strange happening on Mars when they noticed spikes of hydrogen chloride during Martian summer and on the northern hemisphere of the Red Planet. That is both a time and place at which hydrogen chloride shouldn't be detected.

The gas usually peaks in the northern hemisphere during winter on Mars, disappearing in the summer. This variation is connected to the water and dust cycle on Mars. An exception to the rule occurs over volcanic fissures on the flanks of the Alba Mons volcano, in early summer.
The TGO followed up on this by detecting fresh and narrow fissures, in some cases hundreds of feet long, in the Alba Mons region. A clear sign of volcanism.
"It's truly amazing that it spotted a handful of molecules from a perhaps intermittent source, whilst moving continuously along its orbit to monitor the whole Martian atmosphere," Mège said.

The team thinks that these gases have been rising from the interior of Mars during the Martian winter, becoming blocked by ice. When this ice sublimates, changes directly from solid to gas, during summer, the gas is released, prompting spikes in hydrogen chloride seen by the TGO.

"Looking at the spatial distribution of the seeping, it became instantly obvious to me that there was something volcanic behind it, but it had to be demonstrated," said Mège. "A huge part of the work consisted of examining all the possible chemical processes going on in the Martian atmosphere.
"We needed to be rigorous, critical and creative to explain the presence of hydrogen chloride. The data were complex, but also excellent brain food."
Mège and colleagues theorize that the gas is connected to "volcanic plumbing" in the form of a dormant magma chamber under the surface of Mars.

Regions like this could become hotspots (pun not intended) in the search for life on Mars. That is because magmatic gases like hydrogen chloride would have been more abundant in the past, creating a thicker Martian atmosphere and warmer climate.

Not only would this have led to liquid water covering much of the Martian surface, but when lava bubbled through the Martian crust and met groundwater, warm habitable niches ideal for microbial life could have been forged.

"Looking for Martian life in the seeping fissures of the Alba Mons region would make a lot of sense. If hydrothermal systems are active, they could contain the ingredients and energy needed for microorganisms to develop, and shield microorganisms from the hostile and changing environment above the surface," Mège concluded.
The team's research was published in the journal Science Advances on Wednesday (Nov. 4).
