articles.title: NASA's Swift space telescope crashes back to Earth after failed rescue attempt
articles.author: Mike Wall

paras.en: NASA's Swift space telescope has reached the end of its long and winding road.
Swift fell uncontrolled to Earth today (Nov. 4), 22 years after it launched but just three months after a private spacecraft was supposed to boost it to a higher, life-extending orbit.

The 3,200-pound (1,450 kilograms) observatory reentered Earth's atmosphere at 7:39 a.m. EST (1239 GMT) today over northern Sumatra, according to satellite tracker Jonathan McDowell, who cited U.S. Space Force data. The fall likely didn't make much of an impact; NASA officials predicted beforehand that most of the minibus-sized Swift would burn up as it fell, and they put the odds of any of the surviving pieces hurting anyone on Earth at just 1 in 2,100.

Swift — officially known as the Swift Gamma-Ray Burst Explorer — launched to Earth orbit in November 2004 on a two-year mission to study gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), the most powerful explosions in the universe. "Swift" was not an acronym but rather referred to the spacecraft's observational agility.

"Swift needed to detect and locate gamma-ray bursts, communicate their position to other observatories, and then swing its telescopes around to image the burst locations before their afterglows faded out," S. Bradley Cenko, Swift's principal investigator (PI) at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, said in an Oct. 23 statement. "This typically took Swift about a minute to do."

Swift didn't just observe GRBs. It also studied a variety of other cosmic bodies and phenomena, from faraway supernova explosions and feeding black holes to asteroids and comets in our own solar system.

And it kept doing this long after its warranty expired — for about 20 years after, in fact. The space telescope didn't conduct its final science observation until this past Oct. 20. (Swift underwent a name change during this stretch: In 2018, it was rechristened the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory after its first PI, who died the previous year.)

"Swift delivered an incredible, lasting return on investment for the nation, designed for a two-year primary mission but productive for more than 10 times as long," Shawn Domagal-Goldman, director of NASA's Astrophysics Division, said in the same Oct. 23 statement.

"In that time, Swift played a major role in advancing our understanding of the changing universe and was part of a revolution in astrophysics that showed how critical rapid-response observations are to the entire community," he added.

Swift was incredibly productive, observing more than 2,000 GRBs and 1,400 supernovas over the course of its long scientific life. But it could have gathered even more data, had a dramatic rescue mission worked out.

In September 2025, NASA awarded the Arizona company Katalyst Space a $30 million contract to design, launch and operate a robotic spacecraft that would meet up with Swift and boost it to a higher orbit, thus extending its operational life.

Swift was falling back to Earth: It had no onboard thrusters to counteract the effect of atmospheric drag, which had been pulling the observatory down ever since it launched. The process was accelerating as Swift got lower, so Katalyst had to work fast. And the company did: It launched its refrigerator-sized, three-armed LINK servicing spacecraft on July 3, targeting an August capture of Swift.

That didn't happen, however. LINK suffered problems with its propulsion system and orientation-maintaining reaction wheels, which nixed the planned meetup. Still, it was a worthwhile effort, according to NASA.
"From the beginning, this was a high-risk, high-reward mission," Domagal-Goldman said in a statement on Sept. 25, the day that LINK itself crashed back to Earth.

"And while we'll be sad to see Swift's mission come to a close, we knew this boost effort would be worthwhile either way — advancing U.S. spacecraft servicing technology, challenging us to meet unprecedented mission timelines, and testing how we operate satellites to extend their time in low Earth orbit," he added.

Swift's crash today wasn't exactly unusual, by the way. At least three large objects — dead satellites or spent rocket bodies — fall back to Earth every day on average, a 2025 report found. And that number is bound to rise in the coming years, as humanity builds out more and more megaconstellations in Earth orbit.

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. articles.title: 'Trials and Tribble-ations' at 30: The classic 'Star Trek: Deep Space Nine' episode that brought Captains Kirk and Sisko face-to-face
articles.author: Richard Edwards

paras.en: When "Star Trek" celebrated its 60th anniversary in September, it was a strangely muted affair. Sure, there were fan events, screenings, and even an attempt at a world record for the biggest simultaneous Vulcan salute in history, but the lack of a "Doctor Who"-style birthday episode felt like a glaring omission. It was like everyone had shown up for the party, but the organizers had forgotten to book the headline entertainment.

Luckily, there were rather more fireworks for the show's 30th birthday, when both "Voyager" and "Deep Space Nine" marked the occasion in style. "Voyager" episode "Flashback" took Tuvok (Tim Russ) back to his days on the USS Excelsior bridge alongside Original Series vets Hikaru Sulu (George Takei) and Janice Rand (Grace Lee Whitney).

But it was "DS9"'s "Trials and Tribble-ations" that turned out to be the more memorable voyage to "Trek" past, as Captain Benjamin Sisko (Avery Brooks) — with the help of some then-state-of-the-art digital trickery — came face-to-face with a young Captain James T. Kirk (William Shatner).

While "Flashback" aired within days of "Trek"'s September 8 birthday, fans had to wait a little longer for "DS9"'s contribution to the celebrations. Showrunner Ira Steven Behr was keen to avoid disrupting the space station-set drama's story arc for a comedic diversion, meaning that "Trials and Tribble-ations" didn't debut until November 4, 1996.

In the wake of "Flashback" — not to mention Spock and Scotty's comebacks in "The Next Generation" stories "Unification" and "Relics" — the "DS9" writers' room had already decided they needed to take a very different approach.

Early on, "Battlestar Galactica" creator Ronald D. Moore pitched a follow-up to Original Series episode "A Piece of the Action" (aka the one where the residents of Iotia brought 1920s gangsters to life). In an extremely meta concept that predated "Galaxy Quest" by three years, the story would have taken the Enterprise crew to a planet of Kirk and Spock impersonators.

"For the thirtieth anniversary, you go back, and you're basically going back to the planet of 'Star Trek' fans," Moore recalled in "The Fifty-Year Mission" by Mark A. Altman and Edward Gross. "They have conventions; they know all the adventures. It's a phenomenon, and you could comment on 'Star Trek' as a whole. I thought it would be interesting. But [fellow writer] René Echevarria thought it was a dangerous show to do, that we would be talking down to the fans on some level, and perhaps it wasn't the best way to go."
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Instead, Echevarria suggested telling a story in the vein of Woody Allen's "Zelig" or "Forrest Gump" (then a zeitgeisty, multi-Oscar-winning box-office smash) and integrating the "Deep Space Nine" crew with the events of an Original Series episode.

"I thought, 'What bigger treat could there be than to go back into the past and board the original Enterprise and have a mission there?'" Echevarria said in a 1996 making-of documentary. "And Ron immediately said, 'It's gotta be "The Trouble with Tribbles!"'"

"The Trouble with Tribbles", a 1967 episode from "Star Trek"'s second season, is one of the most famous in the franchise's history. As well as featuring some minor scuffles with Klingons, it sees the Enterprise and Deep Space Station K-7 infested with the eponymous tribbles — cute, cuddly furballs of calm that reproduce at a dangerously exponential rate.

In "Trials and Tribble-ations", a timey-wimey incident involving the Bajoran Orb of Time transports the USS Defiant (one of the best "Star Trek" spaceships) back to the era of Kirk and Spock's famous five-year mission.

As Sisko recounts the adventure to a pair of agents from Starfleet's Department of Temporal Investigations (named Dulmur and Lucsly in homage to "The X-Files"), we learn how he, Dax (Terry Farrell), O'Brien (Colm Meaney), and Bashir (Alexander Siddig) spent a day playing Original Series cosplay on Kirk's Enterprise. It's "Star Trek"'s answer to "Back to the Future: Part II", as the crew interacts with established events while taking pains not to mess with history.

Although most of the guest stars from "The Trouble with Tribbles" had passed away over the intervening decades, one actor who'd played a pivotal role was still around. By the time he turned up in "Star Trek", 20-something stand-up comedian Charlie Brill had already brushed shoulders with pop-culture legend, having shared the bill with the Beatles when they made their famous appearance on "The Ed Sullivan Show" in February 1964.

Three years later he'd swapped Lennon and McCartney for Kirk and Spock, playing a Klingon spy masquerading as human Arne Darvin, whose cover is ultimately blown by the famously Klingon-phobic tribbles. In the newer episode, the older Darvin travels back in time to assassinate Kirk, plotting his revenge with a bomb implanted in an unfortunate tribble. Thwarting the evil scheme — and preserving the timeline — forms the basis of Sisko's mission.

Brill's return was seemingly written in the stars. When planning the episode, Behr and the other writers met for lunch at Mulberry Street Pizza in Beverly Hills and noted that the actor was alive and still working in the business. Then, just as they were talking about him, they happened to spot Brill across the very same restaurant.

"What were the chances that we would be talking about this old TV episode from 30 years ago, and the guy who we were talking about to bring back on the show would be standing there ordering a slice of pizza?" Behr recalled at the Trek Talks telethon (via TrekMovie).

But however strong its story, "Trials and Tribble-ations" was always going to live and die by its recreation of ' 60s-era "Trek". The production team subsequently pulled out all the stops, with Behr suggesting at the time that it may have been the most expensive hour of TV ever made.

The actors were kitted out in era-appropriate primary-colored outfits and given '60s hairdos. The make-up team also recreated the appearance of the Original Series' Klingons, whose very different look — "We do not discuss it with outsiders," says Worf — would later be explained away in a "Star Trek: Enterprise" two-parter.

The late Walter Koenig (who'd featured as Chekov in "The Trouble with Tribbles") showed the younger officers how to flip open a communicator, and the stunt team choreographed fights to look like the cheesy, Western-inspired brawls of a bygone era.

Behind the scenes, production designer Michael Okuda and his team used a mixture of original plans and scans of the episodes to painstakingly recreate the sets, while the visual effects team constructed an exact half-scale replica of the original 11-foot Enterprise shooting model housed in the Smithsonian.

The biggest magic trick, however, was dependent on CG technology — then very much in its infancy — making everyone believe that Sisko and co were walking the same corridors as Kirk. VFX supervisor Gary Hutzel had provided proof-of-concept early in the process:

"He showed us a clip from the old show," said Behr. "We looked at it and said, 'Okay, that looks good, but what does that have to do with us?' And he said, 'Well, you see that guy coming in through the door? That's not from the 1967 episode. That's one of our people!'"

Shooting in front of blue- and green-screens, the actors' performances were meticulously matched to the Original Series episode. Early on, Moore had identified two sequences from "The Trouble with Tribbles" that would be perfect for selling the concept: Kirk dressing down a line-up of officers after a bar room brawl and Tribbles raining down on Kirk from a storage container.

O'Brien and Bashir were digitally pasted over the original actors in the former, while the latter was explained away by Sisko and Dax's madcap dash to find the elusive explosive tribble. In most other shots, the DS9ers became background observers in existing scenes.

But there were still debates to be had over whether the two captains should meet. "It led to one of the most vociferous arguments we've had," said Behr, a passionate advocate for the "yes" camp. "We were so deadlocked, and there was so much emotion in the air, we actually turned to the writer intern and said, ‘What do you think?’ End of stalemate. Of course, being an intern and being a smart guy, he sided with his executive producer. And life went on." (The scene in which Sisko hands Kirk a duty roster for approval was actually lifted from another Original Series episode, "Mirror, Mirror", with Brooks replacing Barbara Luna (Lt. Marlena Moreau) on the bridge.)

paras.en: It was all worth the effort. "Trials and Tribble-ations" was the most-watched episode of "DS9"'s fifth season, bagged nominations for three Emmys and a Hugo, and is now widely regarded as one of the best "Trek" episodes of all time.

David Gerrold, who wrote "The Trouble with Tribbles" and appeared as an extra in "Trials and Tribble-ations", described it as "possibly the best episode of 'Star Trek' after the Original Series," and various members of the writers' room have described it as a highlight of their time on the final frontier.

"From the writers to the director to the lighting, costumes, the set, sound effects, visual effects — everybody really put in so much time on that episode to really recreate the original Enterprise in any way they possibly could," said Moore. "Everybody was staring at film clips, doing research into [prop/costume] materials. It was a mania, and everybody just threw themselves into it. They wanted to make it great. And it shows."
'The Trouble with Tribbles' and 'Trials and Tribble-ations' are available to stream on Paramount+ in both the US and UK.

Richard's love affair with outer space started when he saw the original "Star Wars" on TV aged four, and he spent much of the ’90s watching "Star Trek”, "Babylon 5” and “The X-Files" with his mum. After studying physics at university, he became a journalist, swapped science fact for science fiction, and hit the jackpot when he joined the team at SFX, the UK's biggest sci-fi and fantasy magazine. He liked it so much he stayed there for 12 years, four of them as editor.

He's since gone freelance and passes his time writing about "Star Wars", "Star Trek" and superheroes for the likes of SFX, Total Film, TechRadar and GamesRadar+. He has met five Doctors, two Starfleet captains and one Luke Skywalker, and once sat in the cockpit of "Red Dwarf"'s Starbug.

articles.title: Craft Prospect kicks off PERSEUS project to advance optical communications for space
articles.author: Craft Prospect

paras.en: Craft Prospect is working with Fraunhofer Centre for Applied Photonics (Fraunhofer CAP) and Vector Photonics on a new project exploring the potential of next-generation laser technology for high-performance optical communications in space.

PERSEUS (PCSEL Environmental and Radiation Sensitivity: Evaluation for Use in Space) will investigate whether a promising new laser technology called Photonic-Crystal Surface-Emitting Lasers (PCSELs) is suitable for operation in space and can offer a differentiated capability for both space-to-space and space/ground networks.

The project will evaluate the technology under conditions relevant to space deployment, demonstrate its compatibility with representative spacecraft hardware, and identify the next engineering steps required to move towards a commercial solution.

The project is funded through the Advanced Connectivity Technologies (ACT) programme, delivered by Innovate UK and funded by the Department for Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS). The ACT R&D Programme was announced by Minister Ian Murray during his speech at Connected Britain on 9 September 2026.
Exploring a new approach to optical communications

PCSEL technology offers the potential to address some of the limitations of existing optical and RF communications systems in space, supporting the move towards longer-range, higher-capacity, and more secure free-space optical links between ground stations, satellites, and potentially deeper-space assets.
By bridging the gap between component and space system, PERSEUS will chart a course from disruptive technology to differentiated on-orbit capability for the fast-growing space market.
From device testing to spacecraft integration

The PERSEUS programme will subject PCSELs to a range of test campaigns expected of space qualified technologies, as well as carrying out long-range, high-bandwidth free-space demonstrations to showcase early performance.

PCSEL devices will undergo characterisation and testing, including radiation, vibration, and thermal-vacuum campaigns, to better our understanding of how the technology fares in the launch and space environments.

Furthermore, the project will demonstrate early integration success with other flight-representative hardware for end-to-end data transmission, and develop mission concepts that harness the unique capabilities of PCSELs.

The findings will feed into a future communications system design concept and help define the engineering roadmap required to progress PCSEL technology towards a differentiated space communications solution.
Bringing together photonics and space engineering expertise
At Craft Prospect, Head of Engineering Kevin Quillien is serving as Project Lead, supported by Chief Engineer Paul Yarr and Systems Engineers Lauryn Atkinson and Kairavi Pandit.
At Fraunhofer CAP, Dr Gerald Bonner is subcontract lead, while at Vector Photonics Dr Richard Taylor serves as subcontract lead and Dr Graham Goldberg as Project Manager.

The project also builds on Craft Prospect’s growing quantum-optical communications capability, including our work on OPS-SAT VOLT, where we are developing and testing space-to-ground free-space quantum and optical communications technologies as part of our wider mission to deliver Smart Secure Space.
Kevin Quillien, Project Lead and Head of Engineering Craft Prospect, said of the project:
‘PERSEUS is an exciting opportunity to take a promising new photonics technology and understand the potential it has to offer the space industry.

‘By carrying out all the necessary early-stage work to test and characterise PCSELs for space, we will build a strong understanding of the potential that the technology offers in building the next generation of communication solutions. We’re looking forward to working with Fraunhofer CAP and Vector Photonics to explore where this roadmap will take us.’

Craft Prospect is a Glasgow-based space engineering company advancing its vision of Smart Secure Space through onboard intelligence, quantum technologies, and satellite subsystem innovation. Learn more here.
About Fraunhofer Centre for Applied Photonics

Fraunhofer CAP is a not-for-profit research and technology organisation (RTO) offering industry a professional development capability in the fields of photonics, lasers and quantum technologies. Learn more about Fraunhofer CAP here.

Vector Photonics Limited, based in Glasgow, is advancing its revolutionary, proprietary, PCSEL technology from proven R&D and commercial fab environments to high-volume manufacturing. Further information can be found here

articles.title: How to Expand Reliable, Flexible Access to Space
articles.author: Exolaunch

paras.en: The space industry launched more rockets into orbit last year than ever before, yet satellite operators are confronting an unexpected problem: There still aren’t enough rides to go around.
And increasingly, the shortage isn’t simply about the number of rockets.

Satellite companies want launches to more orbital destinations, with more regularity and aboard a wider range of vehicles. Instead, much of the industry has come to depend on a relatively small number of frequently launched rockets that often go to similar orbits. That’s left some companies and their spacecraft waiting months or years for a suitable ride.

“Demand is crazy,” said Robert Sproles, chief executive of Exolaunch, a Berlin-based broker of global launch services that has put 912 satellites into orbit during 51 separate launch events. “The demand curve is so much steeper than the supply curve.”

The squeeze comes despite a historic expansion in launch activity. Data from the FAA shows the agency licensed 187 launches in fiscal year 2026. That’s up from less than 100 a decade earlier and governments are pushing for still more. The Trump administration has called for U.S. spaceports to support more than 1,000 launches and reentries annually by 2030.

But raw launch numbers obscure a problem that is becoming increasingly important as the space economy grows. A rocket going to the wrong orbit at the wrong time isn’t necessarily useful to a satellite operator.
All of that is turning choice, not just capacity, into one of the launch industry’s biggest constraints.
In order to truly close the gap between supply and demand, Sproles said, space transportation companies must also increase the diversity of available launches.

“Yes, we need to meet demand. But we also need to make sure we’re putting that demand in the right places,” he said. “We need to recognize what types of launches are best for what types of missions, and we need to make sure those types of launches are available when the launch customer needs them.”

Market research firm Novaspace reports that the global space economy reached a valuation of $626 billion in 2025. Citing “consolidation, integration, and closer institutional alignment around security, resilience, and operational performance,” it forecasts annual growth of 5.5% through 2034 — at which point it predicts the global space economy will be worth over $1 trillion.
Markets that large are not monolithic, Sproles said, which means the industry needs multiple launch providers operating regularly across different orbital regimes.

“If you rewind to, say, 2016, there was more launch diversity in the market at that time than there is today. There was not more capacity, but there was a wider variety of vehicles that you could reliably gain access to,” Sproles said. The reasons for that decline in launch diversity includes changes in technology, geopolitics, and supply chains since the COVID-19 pandemic, all of which have led to the concentration of launch capacity in a small number of highly active launch providers.
But that variety is necessary, Sproles argues, because launch customers want to be able to optimize for when they can launch, where they need to go, and how much it will cost.

Consider the two most prolific launch providers today: SpaceX — whose Falcon 9 vehicle is optimized for large commercial constellations, human spaceflight, and heavy commercial rideshares — and Rocket Lab, whose Electron vehicle favors small satellites and CubeSats that require custom orbital planes.

“You could not come up with two more different vehicles both in terms of performance and commercial offerings, which just goes to show you that the industry is as hungry for choice as it is for capacity,” Sproles said.

In today’s launch market, rideshare services are a foundation of the space industry. “Rideshare is appropriate when your schedule is flexible enough to align with when a planned rideshare is launching, and when you have enough orbital wiggle room to go where the masses want to go,” Sproles said. “Basically, it makes sense when you have less rigid mission constraints.”

But as missions become more complex and bespoke, one size doesn’t fit all. Rideshare alternatives are needed, including shared launches — where launches are conceived from the outset with multiple customers in mind, instead of one customer’s mission piggybacking haphazardly onto another’s — and dedicated launches, wherein a customer procures an entire launch that’s customized to their unique schedule, destination, and payload, Sproles said
Exolaunch points to four planned missions that underscore the benefits of launch diversity:
- In 2027, the company will conduct a mid-inclination rideshare mission aboard Mitsubishi Heavy Industries’ H3 rocket. It will be the company’s first launch from Japan.

- In late 2027 and 2028, respectively, Exolaunch will launch its Exo-1 and Exo-2 missions aboard two dedicated SpaceX Falcon 9 rockets procured exclusively for an anchor customer that in both instances will use approximately 40% of the launch vehicle; Exolaunch will sell the remaining 60% to other customers seeking a rideshare model.

- In late 2028, Exolaunch will serve as the launch co-integrator for the Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment-Continuity (GRACE-C) mission that is a joint effort of the German Space Agency’s German Aerospace Center (DLR) and NASA. The company will provide a custom structure with which to secure the mission’s payload inside a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket that DLR and NASA had already secured for their launch; in return, DLR and NASA will allow it to provide the rocket’s unused capacity to other customers.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The first eight launches for Exolaunch in 2026 took place across four different launch vehicles from three continents. By securing capacity across a diverse portfolio of launch vehicles, inclinations, and spaceports, Sproles said, Exolaunch gives launch customers not only more predictable access to orbit, but also increased flexibility with regard to cost, schedule, and orbital destination.

Sproles ultimately envisions a future where customers can launch at any time and to any orbit without ever having to consider available launch vehicles or schedules — just as manufacturers in other industries can ship their products knowing that there’s always a container ship, train, or truck available to transport them.

“The ideal situation is that customers don’t have to think about what the vehicle is or when it’s going because there’s always an option to get to the desired orbit at the time when their satellite is manufactured,” Sproles said.
That future is in the hands of launch companies.

“We have multiple launch providers who have shown they can launch rockets. Now, we need those launchers to launch. We need them operating reliably at cadence, and we need them going to multiple orbits. They can do it. We just need them to execute.”

articles.title: NASA Space Grant Students Fuel Agency’s Inspiration Tour
articles.author: Sandra May

paras.en: NASA’s Inspiration Tour spread the excitement of space exploration and aeronautical innovation by connecting the public, industry, and academia with the people, technologies, and organizations that drive American leadership in space. At nearly every stop across the country, NASA Space Grant has brought students into the heart of the action.

In Iowa, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman toured the Make to Innovate program lab at Iowa State University. Students from the Iowa Space Grant Consortium’s Mission Moon program, along with consortium-funded student organizations including Cardinal Space Mining, CySat, and CyLaunch, shared research findings and demonstrated the institution’s strong connection to NASA via agency-funded projects. During a well-attended town hall event NASA experts briefed students on the agency’s Moon Base efforts and how their work can contribute to future exploration.

paras.en: “We’re grateful for the opportunity to welcome NASA leadership to Iowa State,” said Sara Nelson Iowa Space Grant director. “The excitement among students was incredible, and the visit highlighted how the research and innovation happening in Iowa can help advance Artemis and NASA’s future exploration efforts.”

At the University of Arizona, the NASA administrator saw firsthand the space research and engineering capabilities that are enabled by the Arizona Space Grant Consortium. From satellite communications testing to complex optics for peering into deep space to student-built high-altitude balloon payloads and even small satellites, students at the University of Arizona have a long history of contributing to NASA missions and making aerospace career connections. This tour stop also included a Q&A session where the NASA administrator answered questions from local high school and college students.

paras.en: “It was incredible to present the high-altitude ballooning research we do in SEDS (Students for the Exploration and Development of Space) to Jared Isaacman and those at NASA,” said Ella Miller, a junior studying mechanical engineering at the University of Arizona. “Arizona Space Grant has allowed me to get hands-on experience through an entire mission design process every semester, helping me pursue a career in space research and secure internships in this field.”

At the University of Alaska in Fairbanks, the Administrator toured two Geophysical Institute facilities: Poker Flat Research Range, the university’s scientific rocket launching facility, and the Alaska Satellite Facility. During an Alaska Space Grant science fair, students shared research in hibernation biology and showcased CubeSat technology advancements. Students were also able to learn about the agency’s Moon Base program and ask questions about opportunities available to the next generation of innovators and explorers.

paras.en: In North Dakota, the Inspiration Tour focused on future exploration capabilities. Space Grant-funded research at the University of North Dakota is helping to shape the future of exploration across STEM fields. Student fellows and NASA interns shared their projects on supercell mergers using satellite imagery, geomagnetic conditions of aurora borealis, and in-situ resource utilization, to name a few. North Dakota Space Grant STEM ambassador students also shared robotics and drone activities as part of “Mission Moon”, which centers Artemis initiatives in statewide collaborations with educators and other North Dakota colleges and universities.

NASA’s Inspiration Tour will culminate in MAX POWER, a public showcase of air and space innovation on Nov. 7 and 8, highlighting the agency’s commitment to preparing the next generation of innovators and explorers for humanity’s next giant leap. As NASA enters a Golden Age of innovation and exploration, the national network of Space Grant consortia is expanding opportunities for students to lead the way in an aerospace workforce that is evolving and growing. At learning institutions from coast to coast, today’s Space Grant students are launching America’s future in space.

articles.title: NASA Navigation Experiment Shows Promise for Planetary Landings
articles.author: Dede Dinius

paras.en: NASA successfully demonstrated technology designed to help spacecraft autonomously navigate to safe landing sites on the Moon and on other planets.

An Alta-X drone equipped with the agency’s Safe and Precise Landing – Integrated Capabilities Evolution (SPLICE) guidance, navigation, and control payload completed simulated lunar descent and landing maneuvers Aug. 27. The flight took place at Rogers Dry Lake near NASA’s Armstrong Flight Research Center in Edwards, California.

During the tests, the SPLICE payload used an advanced guidance system to map the terrain and assess potential landing areas. If the system determines the targeted landing area is unsafe, the system diverts the drone to a safer location. The system generates high-resolution digital elevation maps from light-detection and sensor data.

Researchers at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston developed the SPLICE payload and partnered with specialists at NASA Armstrong to integrate, test, and fly it aboard the Alta-X drone in June and July. Those tests verified communications, data handling, telemetry, and command- control performance between the SPLICE payload and the drone to prepare for a full-scale test at Voyager Technologies in Mojave, California, later this month.

“This flight test is the culmination of almost a decade of work, for the SPLICE project,” said Davis Adams, NASA project manager. “This flight raised the technology readiness level, priming it for integration into future robotic and crewed lunar flights. Validation of the guidance and navigation systems are applicable to terrestrial, lunar, and Martian descent and landing missions.”

NASA has worked with a number of commercial lunar lander providers to implement iterations of SPLICE into their platforms. A number of the landers slated for upcoming Moon Base missions leverage data collected by NASA through the development of systems like SPLICE to execute soft touchdowns on the lunar surface.

“We are coordinating with industry regarding the usage of the guidance system once the system is available in the NASA software catalog, currently planned for this fall,” Adams said. “Some of the companies also are evaluating the system’s navigation capabilities for precision landing applications, as well as potential extensions for autonomous surface mobility.”

NASA’s Flight Opportunities project, based at NASA Armstrong, enabled flight testing of the SPLICE project early in its development that laid a foundation for it to continue advancing its technology readiness level to what it is today. Flight testing included both a descent altitude and a landing trajectory in 2019 similar to what is expected on a lunar mission and the demonstration of two NASA-developed precision landing sensor systems in 2020.

articles.title: NASA Announces Ka-Band Satellite Relay Awards for Space Communications
articles.author: Jessica Taveau

paras.en: NASA selected three companies on Wednesday to perform work to develop Ka-band space relay capability concepts that are compatible with current missions in space, ensuring service continuity for existing spacecraft without requiring modifications to their onboard systems.
Through this work, NASA will aim to acquire end-to-end solutions that include space, ground, launch, operations, and integration elements, as one of many customers in the commercial marketplace.

The awards, under the Next Space Technologies for Exploration Partnerships-3 Broad Agency Announcement Appendix E, are firm-fixed-price contracts that give NASA the option to provide additional funding up to the award limit to advance from initial concept development and risk reduction to an in-orbit flight demonstration. The initial period of performance runs from Nov. 4 through May 3, 2027, with additional priced options to continue work through 2029.
The contract awardees with maximum potential value inclusive of all future options are:
- Astranis Space Technologies Corp. for $264.3 million.
- Global Enterprise Solutions Inc. for $340.4 million.

Facilitated through the agency’s SCaN (Space Communications and Navigation) program’s Communications Services Project, this work supports NASA’s decision to gradually retire the Tracking and Data Relay Satellite fleet and adopt commercial services for future missions. In addition to the commercial capabilities currently under development by the program’s industry partners, Ka-band services are needed to support select in-orbit missions that cannot feasibly modify flight hardware or transition to non-compatible commercial services.

articles.title: Haiti gang leader seeks UN talks as El Salvador sends 2,000 troops to hunt for missing soldiers

paras.en: Haiti gang leader seeks UN talks as El Salvador sends 2,000 troops to hunt for missing soldiers

A Haitian gang leader wanted by the United States has asked the UN to mediate, as El Salvador sends more than 2,000 troops into the country to search for four of its personnel who went missing after a gang ambush.
Gangs control most of the capital, Port-au-Prince, and have terrorized Haitians for years as they fight over territory and resources.
The UN Security Council-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF) was set up to take on the gangs, protect vital infrastructure and get humanitarian aid moving.
The four Salvadoran military-aviation technicians, who were serving with the force, disappeared during an attack by armed groups on the outskirts of Port-au-Prince on 18 October.
Media reports said the troops El Salvador sent at the end of October are on a mission to rescue them.

Meanwhile, Wilson Joseph – who is one of Haiti's most feared gang leaders – has sent a letter to UN Secretary-General António Guterres calling for dialogue with international forces in the country, presenting himself as an interlocutor ready to negotiate peace.
Mr. Joseph – nicknamed Lanmò Sanjou – leads the 400 Mawozo gang, which is notorious for carrying out kidnappings for ransom.
The UN confirmed on Monday evening that it had received the letter but distanced itself from the contents.

“The receipt of such a letter does not constitute an endorsement of its contents, nor an acknowledgment of its author, nor a position taken by the United Nations,” Stéphane Dujarric, spokesman for the Secretary-General, said in a note to the press.
The Haitian authorities consider the aviation personnel to be missing, while the Salvadorean government believes that they are still alive.

Wilson Joseph's conciliatory stance contrasts dramatically with his organization's past. Located in Croix-des-Bouquets, northeast of the capital Port-au-Prince, 400 Mawozo infamously kidnapped 17 missionaries from the United States and Canada in October 2021.
The FBI is offering a $1 million reward for information leading to Mr. Joseph's arrest.
The GSF is authorised to have 5,500 personnel but the number remains well below that target.
According to UN Spokesperson Stephane Dujarric the “vast majority” of the additional 2,000 Salvadorean troops operating in Haiti “are not deployed under the Gang Suppression Force.”

He added that all “security operations conducted in Haiti, whether under the framework of the GSF or by national authorities and their partners, must be carried out in full accordance with applicable international law, including international human rights law and international humanitarian law.”
Civilians continue to bear the brunt of gang violence in Haiti.
More than 5,700 people were killed or injured between January and mid-September this year, while nearly 1.5 million Haitians were forced to flee their homes, because of violence and insecurity.
According to the UN, around 6.4 million people, more than half of the population, require humanitarian assistance across the country.

articles.title: ‘The world is not ready’: Climate adaptation cash falls far short as warming heads past 1.5°C

paras.en: ‘The world is not ready’: Climate adaptation cash falls far short as warming heads past 1.5°C

Although global warming is set to exceed 1.5°C, financing to help communities adapt to climate change falls far short of needs, the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) said in a report published on Wednesday.
The 2026 Adaptation Gap Report finds that developing countries will require roughly $305 billion annually by 2035 to build resilience and reduce risks.
Yet even if international public adaptation finance triples only a maximum of 29 per cent of needs will be covered.
“The world is not ready to adapt to current climactic conditions, never mind what overshoot of 1.5°C will bring,” warned Inger Andersen, the UNEP Executive Director.
The report was released ahead of the COP31 conference, which opens next week in Antalya, Türkiye.
- global efforts to help developing countries adapt to climate change remain underfunded
- institutional barriers are constraining implementation
- while climate-related losses and damage continue to mount
International public adaptation finance flows reached $28.2 to $31.7 billion in 2024, or just a billion dollars more than the previous year.
Growth is flattening; moreover, the $305 billion estimate excludes the private sector’s own needs, meaning that this figure could double.

The call to triple annual support was agreed at last year’s climate conference in Brazil and is part of a key outcome text known as the Global Mutirão – a Portuguese word based on an indigenous expression for “collective task”.
Even if this goal is achieved, projected funding of $85 billion to $120 billion annually would cover only 20 to 29 per cent of estimated needs after inflation.

“At climate COP31 in Türkiye and beyond, nations must focus on intensifying efforts to achieve the COP30 Global Mutirão aspiration of tripling adaptation finance by 2035 – while understanding that they will need to go even higher to save lives, avoid losses and damages and protect economies,” Ms. Andersen said.
The report stressed that countries could still meet the goal of doubling finance from 2019 levels to $40 billion by 2025 as outlined in the 2021 Glasgow Climate Pact, adopted at COP26 in Scotland.

Multilateral development banks likely increased their financing significantly last year and flows between developing countries have also increased, rising from $3.8 billion in 2019 to $9.6 billion in 2024.

However, finance alone is not enough, and the report underlined the need to strengthen institutions and accelerate implementation to protect vulnerable communities, build resilience and address growing climate-related losses and damage.
Simple health reforms could save 1.6 million lives a year
The UN World Health Organization (WHO) on Wednesday urged countries to scale up six proven climate-resilience measures that it insists could save 1.6 million lives a year.
The appeal comes ahead of UN COP31 climate talks in Türkiye beginning next week.
One of the key messages is that climate change is a health crisis, but much of the harm it causes can be prevented with affordable solutions that are already available.
An estimated 3.3 to 3.6 billion people live in contexts highly vulnerable to climate change.

The six prevention measures that WHO wants to see implemented include early warning systems for heatwaves, water and sanitation services that are resilient to climate change and cleaner household fuels and technologies, for cooking and heating.
The agency is also calling for governments to ensure that fossil fuel prices reflect the damage that they cause to people’s health everywhere.

This could save 1.2 million lives a year from reduced air pollution and have the added benefit of reducing greenhouse gas emissions while generating $5.4 trillion in tax annually, on top of $3 trillion in overall economic welfare gains, annually.

articles.title: Afghan children face narrowing path to education, UN agencies report

paras.en: Afghan children face narrowing path to education, UN agencies report
That’s according to the latest Afghanistan Education Situation report published by the UN’s educational and cultural organization UNESCO and child rights agency UNICEF.
“Afghanistan’s education situation in 2026 is defined by a widening mismatch between strong demand for learning and the capacity of the education system to meet it,” they said.

The school-age population – people aged seven to 18 – grew from approximately 10.4 million in 2019 to 11.5 million in 2024, putting increased pressure on already overstretched schools, teachers and education services.

Recurring emergencies, insufficient investment and large-scale returns of Afghans from Pakistan and Iran are adding to the strain. More than a million returnees arrived this year alone, including more than 245,000 children.

The report notes that education access is deeply unequal as more than 2.6 million girls have been barred from attending school beyond the sixth grade following the return of the Taliban in August 2021.

The few remaining opportunities for learning for teenage girls – such as community-based education, literacy and skills development programmes, distance and digital learning as well as private tutoring – “are far from sufficient”, it stresses.

Although some 5,300 community-driven classes serve around 162,000 learners, with girls accounting for 64 per cent, “nothing can replace in-person schooling and substitute for their fundamental human right to formal education”, the report’s authors note.

Meanwhile, boys’ enrolment has also weakened, resulting in roughly 53 per cent of primary school-age children remaining outside formal general education. This decline is also reflected at the lower and upper-secondary levels, where their participation is 67 per cent and 79 per cent, respectively.

Highlighting incomplete information on private, Islamic and alternative educational provision, the report warns of “an increasingly narrow pathway from primary education into secondary education, tertiary study, skills development and employment”.
Despite the numerous pressures on the educational system, Afghan families continue to seek opportunities for their children to learn, including in areas where schools are inaccessible.
Approximately 6.6 million children enrolled in public primary schools last year, or around 560,000 more than in 2022, but the pace is not keeping up with population growth.

The report also stresses the need to improve education quality and invest in teachers and classroom materials. A nationwide assessment found that less than half of fourth graders reached minimum proficiency in language among eight to nine-year-olds.

With women barred from university, the higher education sector remains substantially smaller than in 2021. Some 208,000 students are enrolled this year, compared with 189,000 in 2024, but still far below the roughly 430,000 in 2020.
The UN agencies are calling for the full restoration of the right to education for Afghan girls and women, and for barriers that undermine the quality of education to be lifted.
They warn that without urgent action, a whole generation will be left behind, which will undermine the country’s future recovery and development.

World Grand Prix champion Luke Humphries continued his Leicester love affair to clinch his fourth Players Championship title of the campaign on Wednesday; you can watch the Grand Slam of Darts in Wolverhampton live on Sky Sports from November 14-22

Luke Humphries stormed to his fourth Players Championship title of 2026 with an 8-4 victory over Niels Zonneveld as Dutch legend Raymond van Barneveld took a huge step towards world championship qualification.
Humphries has now prevailed in three of his four Players Championship appearances in Leicester this season, marking the perfect preparation for the upcoming Grand Slam of Darts.

It was also a terrific day for Van Barneveld, who took a huge step towards world championship qualification with a run to his second ProTour quarter-final of 2026, while Gary Anderson moved him into the provisional Players Championship Finals field with a run to the last four.

"The way I've been the last few weeks, it's an unexpected win for myself," admitted Humphries, who was forced to withdraw from the recent European Championship through illness.

"It was more about coming back and seeing what my energy levels were like, because I've been very ill the past few weeks. I'd never miss a major if I could play. I was devastated. I was on a good run after winning the World Grand Prix.
"Four Players Championship wins, a Euro Tour, the World Grand Prix, a win on the World Series, I've done some good things this year. I think my yearly average is better than it's ever been.

The world No 3 maintained his charge with back-to-back 6-2 victories against Steve Lennon and Gerwyn Price, before defying a 106.75 average from Anderson to triumph in an epic semi-final.

articles.title: Liverpool suffer first CL defeat of season after stunning Fenerbahce comeback

paras.en: Fenerbahce vs Liverpool; UEFA Champions League
Fenerbahce vs Liverpool. UEFA Champions League.
Fenerbahce 3-2 Liverpool: Andoni Iraola's side lose two leads in Istanbul as perfect Champions League start ends

Match report as Liverpool lose 3-2 in their UEFA Champions League game against Fenerbahce in Istanbul; Trey Nyoni and Alexander Isak had put Liverpool ahead twice but poor defending cost the Reds; defeat means Liverpool fail to maintain perfect start in Europe
Liverpool's perfect start to their Champions League campaign came to a sudden halt as they lost two leads in a 3-2 defeat to Fenerbahce in Istanbul.

Goals from 19-year-old Trey Nyoni and Alexander Isak had twice put Andoni Iraola's side ahead, but poor defending saw them hold each of those leads for just four minutes before the hosts completed the comeback late on.
Iraola made five changes to the team that had lost to Arsenal three days prior, opting to rest several big names including Isak and Florian Wirtz.

One of those who remained in the starting XI was Nyoni and he wrote another chapter in his breakthrough season as his deflected volley wrong-footed Ederson and nestled in the back of the net for his first professional goal.
That advantage was cut short as Mason Greenwood's free-kick ricocheted off Jeremy Jacquet and left Alisson just as stranded as his Brazilian counterpart moments earlier.

Isak, Wirtz and Cody Gakpo were sent on in search of the lead, and were rewarded almost immediately. Gakpo's cross gave Isak a free-header inside the six-yard box and the Swede applied the finishing touch with his first touch after being introduced.

It was deja vu for the Reds though, as miscommunication at the back between Gakpo and Alisson allowed former Birmingham academy graduate Archie Brown to tap home another instant equaliser. The defending was even worse as the hosts took the lead shortly after when a sky-high cross was headed home by Vedat Muriqi.

The result is Liverpool's first defeat of their European campaign, halfway through their eight league phase games. Meanwhile, ex-Red masterminds Fenerbahce's first win of their Champions League season.

articles.title: Fake alerts warn of nuclear danger as Ukraine and Russia report emergency app hacks
articles.author: Yuliya Talmazan

paras.en: Nuclear danger, radiation threat and street combat: Ukrainians received a wave of messages Sunday night that raised alarm with a series of grave — and baseless — warnings.

Authorities said the country’s emergency alert application had been targeted in a cyberattack, and hours later Russia said its own alert system had also been hacked. The dueling accusations came just as a rare humanitarian ceasefire between the two sides ended, raising fears of intensified fighting rather than a move toward broader peace.

Residents in Ukraine have become used to the unsettling alerts that buzz their phones with news of incoming Russian missiles and drones — a service millions rely on to seek shelter before the attacks hit their cities. But the warnings Sunday night immediately stood out.
The messages, which began around 10:45 p.m. Kyiv time (3:45 p.m. ET), warned residents not to go outside because of radiation hazard, chemical threat and street fights.
Another message professed, in Russian, that all of Ukraine was under nuclear alert. “Don’t worry,” it added. “Oreshnik is in action,” referring to Russia’s nuclear-capable hypersonic missile.

That message referenced a Telegram channel called Hitcorecorp. Major pro-Kremlin Telegram channel Mash said it spoke with the group and that it took responsibility for the hack. NBC News could not verify who the group is and whether it was responsible for the alerts.

Shortly after the alerts went out late Sunday, Ukraine’s air force said the country’s Air Alert app had most likely been “compromised by the enemy,” confirming there was no “radiation threat” and urging calm.

In separate statements, the app’s creators said “unauthorized third parties interfered with the operation of the app,” forcing them to temporarily suspend its operations. They later called the incident a “cyberattack,” saying it was gradually restoring the service. “The team is carrying out additional measures to protect the app in order to prevent similar situations in the future,” one of the statements said.

Ukrainian media reported that users across the country received the alert, and authorities in the western Lviv region reported that some of the public warning sirens and loudspeaker systems broadcast a “radiation hazard” signal.
“I was outside with my dog when the first alert came,” said Olena Yermakova, 32, a researcher in Kyiv.
She picked up her dog and ran inside, she said, before checking the news to see what was happening.

Because the message was in Russian, “I thought it was a hack by the Russians,” she said. “But the seconds before that were absolutely terrifying. I started running through a checklist in my head of what to do during a nuclear threat and whether I had all the supplies at home, and my hands started shaking.”

Still, many other Ukrainians did not appear unduly alarmed or panicked by the alerts. In fact, many shared memes online, poking fun at what they saw as a blatant fake and the fact the warning was issued in Russian. “No one was particularly surprised,” a user wrote on X. “They might as well have thrown in a dinosaur attack, too.”
The State Emergency Service of Ukraine said Monday the national alert system was operating normally, and an NBC News producer in Kyiv did not experience any further issues with the Air Alert app.

Meanwhile, Russia’s emergencies ministry also said early Monday that its mobile application suffered a “massive cyberattack,” resulting in what it said was “dissemination of fake information to the public.” The public alert system was restored and was operating normally, it said shortly after. It emphasized that the app was only “an additional, supplementary information service.”

Screenshots shared by Russian media and some regional authorities suggested the alert, issued in Russian, warned of “nuclear warheads” launched at Russia. As with the Ukrainian alert, the wording was casual and did not appear official.
Russian authorities did not say who was to blame for the alleged cyberattack, only saying “malicious actors” were behind it.
It was not immediately clear whether the two incidents were linked.
It came just hours after a temporary ceasefire between Kyiv and Moscow came to an end in the occupied southern Ukrainian region of Kherson.

The truce, brokered with involvement from first lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo XIV, held without violations from either side for six days, allowing the evacuation of hundreds of residents from the front-line town of Oleshky, which had been on the brink of a humanitarian catastrophe.
The truce amounted to the biggest de-escalation between Kyiv and Moscow since the war started in early 2022.

“On behalf of America, I commend Russia and Ukraine for their leadership and cooperation surrounding the Oleshky ceasefire,” Melania Trump said in a post on X on Sunday. “I hope Oleshky serves as a foundation for lasting peace between both nations.”

Ukraine’s omsbudsman for human rights, Dmytro Lubinets, said he was exploring opportunities for “further humanitarian initiatives” with his Russian counterpart, Yana Lantratova, adding that it was “important to maintain this mechanism of cooperation.”
Before the truce took hold, the United Nations estimated that 2,000 civilians remained in Oleshky, many experiencing hunger and unable to leave safely because of heavily mined roads.

Neither side has disclosed the exact number of people evacuated, but the first lady said Sunday it was nearly 800. The evacuees could go into territory controlled by either Ukraine or Russia, or remain in the town, officials on both sides said.

Lantratova, the Russian human rights commissioner, said Monday that she had expected more people to evacuate from Oleshky, saying “quite a few empty buses” left the area. Many people chose to stay because they couldn’t leave elderly or sick loved ones, she said, or simply refused to leave their homes no matter what.
She said for those remaining, humanitarian aid deliveries would take place at least monthly, with the “coordination and mediation” of Melania Trump.

Ukraine’s armed forces accused Russia on Monday of using the truce to rotate its units and fortify positions in the area. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that Kyiv also could have used the ceasefire to regroup, calling it a “completely common practice in such situations.”

articles.title: Supermarkets across Europe hit by new fridge cyberattacks
articles.author: Reuters

paras.en: Supermarkets across Europe were hit Monday by a new wave of apparent cyberattacks affecting fridges and freezers.
The incidents caused temperature spikes and spoiled food at stores in Sweden, the Netherlands, Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg and Estonia.

They follow a cyberattack in France last month, in which, police said, hackers seized control of cooling units at hundreds of supermarkets, raising temperatures as high as 122 degrees Fahrenheit and causing fires and food losses.
Authorities have not indicated who could have been behind the incidents. There were no claims of responsibility.
The continent is confronting broader security fears stemming from Russia’s war in Ukraine.
The new cyberattack highlights how digital threats can increasingly affect people’s everyday lives, the European Commission said Monday.

The Ahold Delhaize supermarket chain in the Netherlands told NBC News on Monday that it was aware of an “IT incident” affecting the refrigeration systems in a number of its stores. “Our teams are working hard to fully assess the situation,” it said in an email.

Stephan Moelans, the CEO of the Belgian refrigeration company Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize’s systems, told the Belga news agency that the incident was a cyberattack, in which the units’ evaporators were switched to defrost mode.

A spokesperson for Colruyt Group, which operates Spar stores in Belgium under a franchise system, said five shops’ fridge systems were attacked. The Carrefour supermarket chain in the country said a “cyberattack targeting refrigeration installations only had an extremely limited impact,” affecting 15 of its more than 700 stores.
The Swedish furniture giant Ikea said its store in Mons, Belgium, was also affected.
The “cyber incident” hit the shop’s refrigeration and freezer units, according to a statement sent via email. The company said it was investigating exactly what had happened.
The store in Mons is open to customers, and none of Ikea’s other stores in Belgium have been affected, it said.

Swedish grocery retailer chain ICA also told NBC News that its systems were not affected but that it had been informed of “an incident at a small number of stores that use an external supplier and have their connectivity outside ICA’s central network.”
The incident has affected the stores’ refrigeration and freezer systems, the company said in an email. “ICA is currently supporting the affected stores in managing the incident,” it said.

The ICA Kvantum branch in Sjöbo in southern Sweden wrote on Facebook that its fridges and freezers had been hacked and set to 122 degrees Fahrenheit. It said it was working to discard the affected items.
The privately held grocery retail group Coop told the Swedish daily Aftonbladet that similar incidents had affected six of its stores.
In Ireland, the food wholesaler Musgrave said a cyber incident had affected refrigeration systems in 13 of its SuperValu stores, forcing it to remove some chilled and frozen products from sale.

“Our monitoring systems alerted us to the issue and we took immediate action,” it said in a statement. “Our investigation is ongoing.” The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

In Estonia, a company that makes the affected technology said one of its clients had been hit by a cyberattack in which attackers accessed a computer controlling refrigeration and also turned up the temperature to 122 degrees Fahrenheit, public broadcaster ERR reported.

From refrigerators and heating systems to security cameras and alarm networks, an expanding range of devices can now be monitored and controlled remotely, creating new opportunities for cybercriminals.

Sweden’s national cybersecurity center — which said it could not speculate on who was behind the attacks — is working on several incidents affecting grocery stores across the country, the head of the center, John Billow, said Monday.
“We have in recent weeks ... identified that we have quite a lot of exposed operational technology devices in Sweden that we have been clear about the necessity to update or patch,” he said.

articles.title: U.S. Marine dies in Japan during training, military says
articles.author: Adela Suliman

paras.en: A United States Marine has died in Japan, following a “training incident,” the military said in a statement Wednesday.

The unnamed Marine was undertaking training at Camp Schwab in Okinawa, Japan’s southernmost prefecture, the statement said. The area is home to a large U.S. military presence and bases that serve as a regional hub in the Indo-Pacific.

The Marine who was with the 3rd Marine Division died Tuesday and will not be named until 24 hours after the individual’s family has been notified, the 3rd Marine Division said in a statement Wednesday.
“It is with heavy hearts that 3rd Marine Division announces the death of a Marine following a training incident at Camp Schwab, Okinawa, Japan, on Nov. 3, 2026,” the statement said.
“The circumstances surrounding the incident remain under investigation,” it added. “We express our deepest condolences to the family and loved ones of our Marine.”

Okinawa was under U.S. occupation following World War II until it was handed back to Japan in 1972. Today, the U.S. population on the island is nearly 80,000, with nearly 30,000 being active duty troops from all four branches of the armed forces, though the Marines make up the bulk of the forces.

Separately, Secretary of State Marco Rubio last month pledged to cooperate with Japanese authorities investigating allegations that a U.S. Marine murdered a woman in Okinawa. The case sparked widespread protests and led to a U.S. military curfew and mandatory training in standards and discipline.
Lt. Gen. Benjamin Watson, commander of the III Marine Expeditionary Force, said at the time that serving on the Japanese island “comes with responsibility.”

articles.title: Live: Education ministers consider screen time and generative AI limits in schools
articles.author: Joshua Boscaini

paras.en: Federal politics live: Education ministers consider screen time and generative AI limits in schools
Education ministers have agreed to consider imposing screen time limits and restrictions on kids using generative AI at schools across the country.
Follow all the updates in our live blog.
Education ministers agree to look at school screen time limits
Screen-time limits and limits on kids using generative AI will be considered at schools across the country as part of a push to improve education outcomes.
The move follows international testing which, earlier this year, revealed Australian students' reading and maths have been going backwards over the past 20 years.
The same tests, by the Programme for International Student Assessment, found Australian school kids spend more time using devices than kids in other OECD countries.
At a meeting of the nation's education ministers earlier this week, they agreed to set, or at least consider, screen-time limits.
Under the plan a digital detox taskforce will be established to lead the charge on cutting down on the use of devices in schools.
"We're announcing the next stage of reforms to help our kids learn and to support our teachers," Federal Education Minister Jason Clare says.
The education ministers also agreed to change the maths curriculum for primary school students and improve the way kids learn about antisemitism.
"Schools don't just teach numeracy, literacy and critical thinking skills. They also build character," Clare says.

Let's get right into this and see where it leads us!

articles.title: Opetaia moves to heavyweight to fight former world champ Wilder

paras.en: Jai Opetaia will move up to the heavyweight division to face former world champion Deontay Wilder.
The fight will be on the undercard of the all-British heavyweight showdown between Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua.
The fight will be in Cardiff and on Netflix on Friday, December 11, local time.
Jai Opetaia has been handed the fight of his life as he gambles on moving up to heavyweight to take on thunder-hitting former world champion Deontay Wilder.

Australia's unbeaten cruiserweight maestro, a contender for the sport's best pound-for-pound fighter, will move into uncharted waters by tackling the explosive American veteran on the undercard of the blockbuster Tyson Fury-Anthony Joshua show at Principality Stadium on December 11 in Cardiff.

Wilder is now 41 and perhaps not the destructive force of old, but taking on one of the biggest hitters the sport has witnessed still represents a daring gamble for Opetaia, 10 years his junior, as the world-beating Gold Coast-based southpaw and The Ring Magazine champion protects his perfect 31-fight record.
It is the first major fight above the 200-pound division for Opetaia, with his promoter Dana White admitting: "It's a very dangerous fight for him considering where he sits in his division right now.
"But he's a fighter; he'll fight anybody, even at heavyweight with a guy who hits as hard as Wilder does."
It looks poised to be a one-off, with Opetaia likely returning to cruiserweight afterwards to chase a showdown with American David Benavidez, the division's other major unbeaten force.

Last time out in Nevada in September, Opetaia stopped Noel Mikaelian in the ninth round and called out ringside observer Benavidez, whose heritage has earned him the nickname the "Mexican Monster", with the request: "Respectfully, let's get it on.
"That's the fight Jai really wants, so we've got to figure that one out," White said.
"He wants to stay active, he wants to fight, and he doesn't care if it's at heavyweight or wherever. He's ready to go."

Wilder, though, is by far the biggest name Opetaia will have faced, a champion who held the WBC belt for five years between 2015 and 2020 and who had an epic trilogy of fights with Briton Fury, coming off worse twice after an extraordinary draw in their first bout.

But he has lost four of his last seven contests and, in his last outing, had to battle to earn a scruffy points win over British contender Derek Chisora in London in April, leaving his career record at 45 wins, four losses and a draw.

The all-British bill-topper between Fury and Joshua is being sold as the biggest night of boxing ever witnessed in the UK, with tickets in Cardiff going within an hour of going on sale and the bill being screened globally on Netflix.

articles.title: Woman taken into foster care as a child now helping others
articles.author: Piper Duffy

paras.en: When Rose Taylor reflects on how different her life could have been if she had not met the teacher who became her foster carer, she is overcome with emotion.
"I genuinely wonder if I would still be alive at 43."
The Newcastle-based woman spent her formative teenage years in foster care placements and refuges, and was homeless before she experienced stable living.
Now, decades later, Ms Taylor works at the coalface of that same system, which is experiencing a national shortage of carers.
She said her story demonstrated how important it was for more people to step up.
When she was 12, Ms Taylor left for school one day unaware she would not return home.
Strangers, who she later learned were foster care case managers, took her out of class without warning and told her she was not safe living with her parents.
"I was absolutely terrified," Ms Taylor said of being placed into emergency care.
By the time she was almost 16, she had shifted between five foster care placements, two refuges and a semi-independent living program.
Left feeling unwanted and hopeless, the teenager felt she was better off alone living on the streets, and stopped telling the child welfare authorities her whereabouts.
"If I couldn't have my family, I wanted nobody," Ms Taylor said.
"I lived with this false facade that I was hardened, and I didn't care.
"But I can tell you I never cried more or felt more scared than the time I was living on the streets of Parramatta and Liverpool in Sydney as a 15-year-old."
Despite being homeless, Ms Taylor found "solace in school" and turned up each day.
When other students went home to their parents, she would find a place to roll out her sleeping bag and hang her uniform over a park bench for the night.
Ms Taylor had been living on the streets for weeks when someone took notice.
"I had a teacher who saw through [the facade] and could see I was trying to tell the world something," she said.

"When I would blow-up and storm out of a classroom, this teacher would turn up in the playground or wherever I was, sit with me and say, 'What's happening? Are you okay?' Which are questions no-one had asked."
Eventually the teacher found another colleague to care for Ms Taylor full time, and together they took her under their protective wing.
"It's not like they walked into my life and I was magically better … [but] while I was working things out they just approached me with care, curiosity and gentleness," she said.
After more than a year of stability with both teachers as her caring guardians, Ms Taylor started to see a brighter future and finished her schooling.
"I had a hard time [at 15] seeing beyond a week, let alone doing the HSC and seeing what the future looks like … that was enormous," she said.
Data from the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare shows as of June 30, 2021, there were about 9,000 foster care households across the country.
However, by June 2025, that number had dropped to about 5,900.
Life Without Barriers, which connects young adults and children with a safe environment, said about 45,000 children across Australia needed care.
The not-for-profit's youth and family services boss in New South Wales, Deanne Carroll, said cost-of-living pressures had contributed to a national carer shortage.
"I think since COVID we've seen a lot of societal changes … which has meant becoming a foster carer has become out of reach for some people,"
"There's a whole range of impacts, but generally it seems to correlate with cost-of-living increases, which has impacted directly on our need for carers."
Ms Taylor, now 43 and with a family of her own, is using her upbringing to enlighten people about how they can make a difference in a child's life.
For the past decade, she has worked as an operations manager at Life Without Barriers in Newcastle, helping recruit people who could be well-suited for foster caring.
"We've got a national foster carer shortage, which is really why I've decided to speak up," Ms Taylor said.
"At the end of the day [these children] are our future adults, our future leaders, and we can all play a role [in helping]."

articles.title: Jimmy Kimmel roasts Trump in late night monologue amid 'blue tsunami' midterms
articles.author: Alexandra Mae Jones

paras.en: Jimmy Kimmel roasts Trump in late night monologue amid 'blue tsunami' midterms
Trump has repeatedly called for Kimmel to be fired by ABC
Late night host Jimmy Kimmel had some choice words for U.S. President Donald Trump last night as a “blue tsunami” stormed the country during the U.S. midterm elections.

Kimmel, host of ABC’s Jimmy Kimmel Live!, dragged the president through the verbal mud in his monologue Tuesday night, in a clip that has since racked up more than 8 million views as of Wednesday afternoon.
“Trump was reportedly angry and cursing as the results came in,” he said. “Word from inside the White House is he’s already run out of dipping sauce containers to throw at the television set.”
He added, “the blue wave made landfall, and now the Red Wedding begins,” referencing a famous massacre in the HBO show Game of Thrones.

No major late-night shows aired live during the election results, but Kimmel’s show was taped later in the night than usual, around 7 p.m. in Los Angeles, so that Kimmel could react to the early results.

“After all the talk about Nicki Minaj’s ass, John Husted’s ass, the only ass on Trump’s mind tonight is the one that just got handed to him,” Kimmel said, referencing Trump’s perplexing comments in recent weeks fixating on the gluteal physique of colleagues.
Jimmy Kimmel poses with the award for outstanding host for a game show for Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? during the Emmys in 2026, in Los Angeles. (Chris Pizzello/The Associated Press)
“Democrats have officially taken the House, thanks to President Trump. Blob Vila flipped another house.”
The night saw Democrats retake the House and the Senate, winning several key races and flipping seats long held by Republicans.

Although the full results aren’t in yet, the Democrats have already gained seven seats in the Senate, 25 seats in the House, and five seats among governors, according to The Associated Press, making for a historic midterms for the U.S.
Leading up to the midterms, Trump frequently urged his supporters to “pretend I am on the ballot” in a bid to rally his base.
- Updated Trump strategy unchanged after Democrats' midterm landslide, says Canada-U.S. trade minister
- Until the midterms, only 3 Black governors were ever elected in U.S. Tuesday saw 5 wins
- Analysis What the Republican midterm defeat means for Trump, the U.S. and Canada
He struck a different tone on the phone to Fox News as the results came in, claiming that the sitting president always loses the midterms, and taking no responsibility for the Republican defeat.
“I shouldn’t feel guilty, because virtually … no matter how good the president is, you lose. I don’t know why. Nobody’s explained that,” he said.

He has blamed losses on lackluster candidates, even though Trump himself had endorsed or selected many candidates who suffered historic losses in areas long thought to be safe Republican seats. Trump hand-picked Darline Graham to replace her late brother Lindsey Graham as Senator in South Carolina, but she lost to Democrat Annie Andrews in an upset. Trump also endorsed Ken Paxton for Senator in Texas, only for James Talarico to make history as the first Democrat elected to the Senate in Texas in nearly 40 years.
