articles.title: JD Power says total losses weigh on insurance customer satisfaction
articles.author: Lurah Lowery

paras.en: Auto insurance customer satisfaction with claims handling practices depends on repairability, according to a new study from JD Power.
According to the 2026 U.S. Auto Claims Satisfaction Study, total loss determinations decrease overall customer satisfaction by 12 points.

The study shows that overall customer satisfaction with the auto insurance claims process improves 4 points (on a 1,000-point scale) when damages are repairable. This is the third consecutive year of declining satisfaction for total loss claims, declining 46 points since 2023.

Overall, 26% of auto insurance claims were classified as total losses in 2026, up from just 16% four years ago. JD Power notes that vehicle repairs have become more costly, more customers are keeping their vehicles on the road longer, and higher deductibles are removing smaller repairs from the claim process.

The overall auto claims customer satisfaction score is the same as last year at 700. Amica ranks highest in overall customer satisfaction at 775, followed by Nationwide (743) and Automobile Club of Southern CA (AAA) (740).

“A complex mix of trends are conspiring to make this an incredibly challenging market environment for managing auto insurance claims customer satisfaction,” said Mark Garrett, JD Power’s director of global insurance intelligence, in the press release.

“On the positive side, rates are coming down and repair cycle times have improved dramatically, so customers who can have their vehicles fixed are showing high levels of satisfaction with the claims experience. However, persistent affordability challenges have many customers keeping vehicles longer or making changes to their policy, such as dropping rental coverage or taking on higher insurance deductibles. Additionally, many customers are upside down on their auto loans, which means the payoff in a total loss scenario can be less than they owe on their vehicles. All of these can make for a poor customer experience in the event of a total loss.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Total loss customer satisfaction scores are lowest (490) when insurer payouts don’t cover what the customer still owes on their vehicle loan, according to the study. Among total loss customers with vehicle loans, 25% received payouts that were less than what they owed.
JD Power notes that repair cycle times are improving, down to 15.3 days through Q1 and 10 days less than in Q1 2024.
In August, Enterprise Mobility reported that the overall length of rental (LOR) for collision-related rentals in Q2 2026 was 15.1 days, the same as Q2 2025.

Overall customer satisfaction scores are highest (804) when customers completely agree that their insurer provided a seamless experience across channels. Satisfaction scores are lowest (390) when customers disagree with that statement. Disagreement often comes from not understanding explanations, using multiple channels to ask questions, or digital tools not working as expected, according to JD Power.
“Currently, insurers are delivering a seamless cross-channel experience just 54% of the time, one of the lowest-performing key performance indicators in the study,” JD Power says.

The study examines trust, fairness of settlement, people, time to settle a claim, communication, ease of resolving a claim, ease of starting a claim, and digital channels in auto claims experiences of customers from the largest insurance providers across the U.S.

The 2026 study is based on survey responses from 8,261 auto insurance customers who settled a claim within the past nine months before responding to the survey. The survey was fielded from September 2025 through August 2026.

articles.title: UPDATE Cox Automotive VinSolutions, Honda investigate suspicious cyber activity
articles.author: Lurah Lowery

paras.en: Following publication, Honda provided an update to Repairer Driven News:

“After restoring iN services, we experienced technical challenges and took the system back offline. As we work to address these challenges, our top priority is to restore services as quickly as possible. As we continue to strengthen the environment, there could be intermittent outages over the next several days.”

Cox Automotive confirmed Friday that it recently “detected suspicious activity” in VinSolutions, its CRM and sales software, while Honda said it is investigating a separate recent cybersecurity incident. Neither company provided dates of the incidents.

“Customers can continue to engage with all Cox Automotive solutions as they normally would. We are working diligently with outside cyber experts to determine the nature and scope of any data that was involved. Based on our investigation so far, we believe this affected a limited subset of our VinSolutions dealers and will notify any affected parties directly and in line with our obligations. Our top priority is supporting our dealers’ businesses and preserving the trust we’ve earned from them for decades.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: CBT News reported Oct. 27 that hackers, calling themselves Scarlett Group, posted “claims” involving VinSolutions online Oct. 23.

“However, Cox hasn’t confirmed those claims, and they remain unverified,” the article states. “Ransomware.live recorded Scarlett Group’s listing of VinSolutions on its leak site Friday [Oct. 23], describing the group as newly active and saying its claims should be treated with caution until independently verified. Dark web monitoring service Darkwiser reported that the group claims to have customer records, including Social Security numbers, driver’s license numbers, and credit applications. Notably, Darkwiser labeled the claims unverified, and Cox hasn’t confirmed any data types or published a record count.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Honda confirmed to RDN that it recently experienced a cybersecurity incident involving its Interactive Network (iN).

“As a precaution, Honda temporarily took the iN offline to allow for a proper investigation and ensure the protection of our system,” Honda spokesperson Chris Naughton told RDN on Friday. “At this time, we have not identified evidence that customer information was accessed, and our investigation remains ongoing. Honda was able to safely restore iN services on Wednesday (10/28/26).”

A collision repair shop received an email on Oct. 29 from a Honda dealership saying that a cybersecurity attack compromised Honda iN, preventing more than 1,100 dealerships nationwide from checking inventory availability and placing new parts orders.
Separately, an anonymous tip provided to RDN indicated some collision centers have been compromised through email links, allowing threat actors to access CCC’s estimating and management systems.

They said once the link is clicked, threat actors access and change passwords in the systems, then use them to contact insurance companies posing as collision centers, saying the customer removed the vehicle, or that the insurance company should just pay the customer, and provide updated account information.
They’ve also reportedly called an insurance company, posing as the customer, and said they aren’t getting the vehicle repaired and want to cash out.
CCC didn’t confirm or deny the tip. However, CCC shared information about the security advisories it provides to shops to help protect themselves.

“This is an important topic,” said Michelle Hellyar, CCC spokesperson. “Email phishing, social engineering, and impersonation scams are an increasing threat across industries. Like many technology providers, CCC periodically shares security advisories and best practices to help customers recognize and avoid these attacks. These advisories are preventive in nature and not prompted by a compromise of CCC’s systems.

“In our advisories, we encourage businesses to use multi-factor authentication, never share passwords, exercise caution with unexpected requests involving sensitive information or payment changes, and independently verify those requests through established, trusted contacts before taking action.”
Last year, IT services company StoredTech simulated the ramifications of a fictional cybersecurity attack on an auto repair shop for attendees of a Collision Industry Conference (CIC) meeting.

In the scenario, the owner replied to an email that he thought was from his trusted supplier, “Tool Titans.” The email asked for information to complete a tool order and included multi-factor authentication.
Allan Polak, StoredTech senior of technology, said the hackers threatened to permanently delete all of Bob’s data and leak it to the dark web if half a Bitcoin wasn’t paid within 72 hours.
Polak guided the audience through Bob’s decision to pay the ransom after three days of no business operations.

“Threat actors used the stolen passwords to gain access to multiple computers in Bob’s office, and they gained access to other resources, like phones, cloud, files, et cetera,” Polak said. “And once they gained access to those computers, they also found an Excel spreadsheet. That Excel spreadsheet was a treasure trove. It had all kinds of passwords for them, including some personal accounts, and they use that to just gain a larger foothold and go deeper and deeper.”

articles.title: Make Professional Development a Priority in 2027
articles.author: Brady Netzel

paras.en: Automotive educators spend their careers preparing students for the future. But as the automotive industry continues to evolve, preparing the next generation of technicians also means making time for their own professional development.

From electric vehicles and advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) to increasingly complex diagnostic technology, today’s automotive classrooms must keep pace with an industry that rarely stands still. At the same time, instructors are balancing curriculum requirements, student engagement, limited resources, and the everyday demands of running an effective automotive program.

As educators begin looking ahead to 2027, professional development deserves a place in that planning. Not simply as a requirement to fulfill, but as an opportunity to strengthen their skills, connect with fellow instructors, and bring new ideas back to their students.

The vehicles entering today’s service bays are not the same vehicles students were learning on a decade ago. As technology advances, automotive educators face the ongoing challenge of deciding what to introduce into their programs and how to teach it effectively.
Professional development helps instructors stay connected to these changes while building the knowledge and confidence needed to introduce emerging technologies into their classrooms.

That might mean learning a new diagnostic approach, exploring how high-voltage systems can be incorporated into existing lessons, or discovering a more effective way to demonstrate a complicated electrical concept.
But staying current isn’t only about technical knowledge. It’s also about finding better ways to help students understand and apply that knowledge.
At the 2026 Automotive Educators Conference (AEC), Craig Winkler of Wake Tech Community College highlighted the value of having a “great mix between technical and teaching classes offered.”
That balance is important. Automotive educators need opportunities to develop both their technical expertise and their ability to translate that expertise into meaningful learning experiences.
The Value of Learning From Fellow Educators
Some of the most valuable professional development happens through conversations with people who understand the challenges of teaching automotive technology.
Whether discussing student engagement, classroom management, curriculum development, or program resources, fellow educators can offer perspectives that are difficult to find elsewhere.

An instructor at one school may have discovered a successful approach to a challenging lesson. Another may have found a creative way to introduce new technology using existing equipment. Sharing those experiences gives educators an opportunity to learn from one another rather than approaching every challenge independently.
Jacob Johnson of Box Elder High School reflected on this value following AEC 2026:
“It’s always good to be able to hear and discuss the challenges and successes of others as well as collect new ideas and methods to improve all aspects of teaching.”
Johnson also shared that he had successfully implemented several methods learned from a fellow educator.

That is one of the strengths of educator-focused professional development. It creates opportunities not only to gain knowledge but also to develop relationships that can support instructors long after a training session ends.
Finding Professional Development That Makes a Difference
Industry training, manufacturer programs, webinars, educator roundtables, and professional networks all provide valuable ways to continue learning.
The key is identifying opportunities that address the needs of both the instructor and their program.

For automotive educators, that often means seeking training that combines current technical information with practical classroom applications. Learning about an emerging technology is valuable, but discovering how to incorporate that knowledge into a lesson or lab can make the experience even more meaningful.
The Automotive Educators Conference brings those elements together through technical training, instructional strategies, hands-on learning, and collaboration with educators from across North America.

Built around the principle “For Automotive Teachers, By Automotive Teachers,“ AEC recognizes that teaching automotive technology requires a unique combination of industry knowledge and educational expertise.
It also provides an opportunity to connect with industry partners and explore resources that can support program development and student preparation.
Make Professional Development Part of Your 2027 Plans

Finding time and resources for professional development isn’t always easy. Between teaching schedules, program responsibilities, and limited school budgets, opportunities for training can quickly become an afterthought.

As you look toward 2027, consider which areas of your program could benefit most from additional training. Are there emerging technologies you want to understand better? Teaching strategies you’d like to explore? Challenges that could benefit from the perspective of other automotive educators?
Identifying those needs early can help you prioritize opportunities, explore available funding, and begin conversations with administrators about professional development goals for the coming year.
It also helps ensure that the training you pursue aligns with what matters most to you and your students.
Investing in your professional development is also an investment in the students who depend on you to prepare them for their future careers.

As you begin planning for 2027, consider making the Automotive Educators Conference part of your professional development goals. With opportunities to strengthen your technical knowledge, exchange ideas with fellow educators, and discover practical approaches to teaching, AEC offers an experience designed around the people who teach automotive technology every day.
Because preparing students for what’s next starts with educators who never stop learning.
Explore the Automotive Educators Conference and start planning your professional development for 2027.

articles.title: How Do We Recruit the Next Generation of Technicians?
articles.author: Christian Hinton

paras.en: The automotive industry faces a growing workforce challenge, making automotive technician recruitment increasingly important for repair shops. A wave of experienced technicians is nearing retirement, while the number of incoming workers is not large enough to replace them.
The industry needs tens of thousands of jobs filled each year. At the same time, training programs are not producing enough graduates, and Americans are keeping their vehicles longer.
Shops looking to close the labor gap need to reach the next generation of workers earlier and more effectively.
Automotive Technician Recruitment Can Reach New Candidates
Recruiting the next generation of technicians starts with reaching candidates where they are. That can include groups shops may not traditionally consider, such as recent college graduates.

Many young people are leaving college and entering a crowded job market. Some graduates may be open to different career paths, particularly those offering competitive pay, stability and an in-demand skill.
Employee-sponsored training and formal apprenticeship programs can help provide that path.
Job Postings Should Explain the Purpose of the Work

Younger workers also want to understand the purpose behind their work. They want to know who they are helping and why their role matters. For that reason, job postings should communicate more than the availability of an automotive technician position.

Cars are part of everyday life, and technicians help keep people moving. Shops are hiring employees who play a role in keeping vehicles on the road. Communicating that purpose can help candidates understand the broader value of the job.
Workplace Culture Can Support Technician Retention

Many young workers are accustomed to having options and experiencing rapid change. If a workplace does not meet their expectations, they may choose to leave rather than remain in the position. That makes workplace culture an important part of technician recruitment and retention.

Shops can build stronger relationships by taking an interest in employees’ lives and creating opportunities for teams to connect. Team events can also help employees become more comfortable with one another and feel more connected to the shop.
